## Are Keyless Entry Systems Worth It for a Small Business?

Source: https://deluxelocksmiths.com/blog/keyless-entry-small-business-worth-it/

By the Deluxe Locksmith team October 9, 2026

Keyless entry pays off when staff change often. Here is when it fits, when plain keys still win, and the exit door rule.

Sometimes, yes. Keyless entry earns its keep when keys have gotten out of hand, and it's a waste when they haven't. Staff who keep turning over, a stream of vendors, a manager asking who locked up last night: those are the signs. But three trusted people sharing one storefront door? Honestly, plain keys are probably fine.

Skimming? Here's the gist. Electronic access swaps copies of a metal key for credentials you can switch off, and it pays off when access changes a lot. It won't fix a flimsy door. A code everyone shares can't tell you who came in. And an exit door still has to let people out. Answer three quick questions below and you'll know which way to lean.

Key Takeaways

- You're buying control: end one person's access without new hardware or a hunt for copies.
- One shared code is easy, but it can't say who walked in. Give people their own.
- Exit-door hardware has to release with no more than 15 pounds of force under NFPA 101 (Decoded: Which doors need panic hardware?, I Dig Hardware, Allegion, 2026).
- Look for electrified locks certified to ANSI/BHMA A156.25 (A156.25 Electrified Locking Systems, BHMA, 2023).

### What is a keyless entry system?

A keyless entry system is a lock that opens with something other than a metal key. Keypad code, card, fob, phone. You add a person, you take a person off, and the lock itself never gets touched. Some systems log every entry. The bigger ones tie a bunch of doors to one list, so a single person runs the whole building.

Honestly, "keyless" oversells it. Somebody still manages the credentials, and most buildings stash a metal key somewhere for emergencies. What changes is how many copies are floating around, and how fast you can cut someone off. We install several kinds, and our keyless entry systems page lists them.

### The 3-Question Keyless Test

Whether it's worth it boils down to three questions. We call it the 3-Question Keyless Test. It works for a one-door shop and for an office with five.

- How often does access change? Count everyone who's held a key this year. Then count how many don't need one now. Seasonal help, cleaners, contractors, the delivery driver, the cousin who covered a weekend once... it adds up fast. Almost never? Keep your keys. Every few months? Keep reading.
- Do different doors need different answers? Owner gets everything. Cashier gets the front. A vendor gets the back door on Tuesdays, and that's it. Keys can't do that, so everybody gets the same yes.
- Do you ever need to know who came in? Usually this matters after something goes wrong. A break-in, a missing delivery, a fight over who forgot to lock up. A shared code leaves you guessing. Individual codes, cards and fobs usually don't.

Two or three yeses point toward electronic access. Zero or one points toward keys, done well.

### When are plain keys still the right call?

Plain keys still win for one location, a small steady team and a door or two. They don't need power or software, they work in a blackout, and nobody has to learn anything new. A solid deadbolt with a restricted keyway can beat a fancier setup.

Not sure you need electronics at all? Often the real problem is that nobody knows who holds copies. Rekeying and moving to a restricted key system fixes that without any electronics, and we walk through how in our guide to master key systems for multi-door businesses.

Electronic access makes sense when the headache keeps coming back. Rekeying every time somebody leaves? That's the kind.

### Choosing a credential for your door

Not every credential suits every business. Here's how the three common types compare on a small commercial door.

Credential |
How it works |
What you can see afterward |
Main weak spot |
Best fit |

Keypad code |
Staff type a code |
Nothing with one shared code. Per-person entry only if each person has their own |
Codes get shared or written down |
One or two doors, a few trusted staff |

Card or fob |
Staff tap a card or fob |
Which credential opened which door, on systems that keep a log |
Cards and fobs get lost |
Several doors, or people who come and go |

Phone credential |
Staff open the door from an app |
Which person entered, on systems that keep a log |
Depends on phones and accounts staying current |
Teams already run from a phone |

If you're unsure, start with a keypad that gives each person their own code. Cards and fobs make sense once you have more people and more doors. Phones are handy, though they add an app and an account to keep up. Whatever you choose, the lock should be commercial grade, sized to your door, and certified to ANSI/BHMA A156.25, the standard for electrified locking devices. BHMA keeps a directory of certified products (A156.25 Electrified Locking Systems, BHMA, 2023).

### What happens when the power goes out?

An electric lock has to pick a side when the power dies. Fail-safe means it unlocks. Fail-secure means it stays locked. Neither is "better," you just need to choose on purpose.

A stockroom full of stock usually wants fail-secure, so a blackout doesn't leave the door hanging open. A door people rely on to get out of the building? Different story, and the next section covers it. Panic hardware still lets someone push through from the inside even when the outside is locked.

Most battery keypads keep a metal key override for dead batteries. Ask about it before you buy. Ask who changes the batteries, too, and how often. Then pull the plug, or the batteries, and test the door. An electric lock should never stop someone from leaving by hand (How to Install a Panic Bar, National Lock Supply, 2025).

### Can you add electronic access to an exit door?

Yes, but this is where owners get tripped up. A door that needs panic hardware, the push bar people hit on the way out in an emergency, plays by tougher rules than an office door. NFPA 101 requires that hardware to be listed to ANSI/BHMA A156.3, the exit device standard, and the force to unlatch it can't top 15 pounds (Decoded: Which doors need panic hardware?, I Dig Hardware, Allegion, 2026).

Short version. Electronic access decides who comes in, and it never gets a say in who goes out.

If you're eyeing a keypad or badge reader on a door with a push bar, plan both at once. The 2024 code changed how an electric lock on a panic door can release, and an installer who only handles one half can get it wrong. We cover it in Does Your Cecil County Business Need a Panic Bar?, and our panic bar installation page covers the hardware itself.

### What goes wrong after installation?

The hardware rarely fails first. The habits around it do.

Start with shared codes. One code for the whole crew works great until somebody quits, and then it's a copied key in disguise. Codes end up on sticky notes, too. Give everyone their own, or change the code every time a person leaves.

Lost cards and fobs come next, and every credential someone can lose needs a plan. That starts with knowing who holds each one. When one goes missing, switch it off the same day.

Then there's the owner problem. Pick one person to add and remove access. When everybody's in charge, nobody is, and people who left months ago are still on the list.

Fit matters. A lock that's perfect for a wood office door can flat-out fail on an aluminum storefront, where the frame, the glass and the swing of the door all get a vote.

And then there's wiring. A battery-only keypad is simple. Anything tied into power, a controller or your network needs an actual plan, because mistakes show up as flaky doors and gaps in the entry record.

### What we check before recommending a system

We look at more than the lock. Door and frame come first, since new hardware has to fit what's already there. Wood, hollow metal and aluminum all behave differently. Aluminum storefront doors are the fussy bunch, because narrow stiles leave barely any room for a lock body. And how the door hangs matters. One that sags or drags will fight an electric strike every day.

After that, how many people need access, and how often that changes. Same three questions as the test, just out loud.

Most owners skip the end of the day. Who locks up? Who gets in at night? What happens when the power's off or a battery dies? If a system only works on a good day, it isn't finished.

A typical visit goes like this:

- Walk every door that will use the system. Note the door, the frame, and whether it's an exit.
- Settle who needs which door, and how that list is likely to change.
- Pick the credential and the power-loss behavior, door by door.
- Install, program and test each one, with the power off too.
- Leave you a plain list of who holds what, and how to add or remove someone.

Doors in Elkton or elsewhere in Cecil County? We do this on site. Our Elkton keyless entry page shows what that looks like locally.

### Frequently Asked Questions

### Are keyless entry systems secure?

Depends what you mean. The lock only does so much. A flimsy door or a soft frame beats any keypad, and one code shared by the whole crew isn't secure in any way that matters. Solid door, good lock, separate credential per person? That's hard to beat.

### What happens to a keyless lock when the batteries die?

Usually you get a warning first, a blinking light or a beep, long before they quit. Plenty of locks keep a regular key cylinder as a backup too. Have your installer show you the override, and put battery swaps on somebody's calendar. A dead-battery lockout is the avoidable kind.

### Can I add keyless entry to a door with a panic bar?

Often, yes. People still need to walk out with no key, no code and no thinking, though, and your local code spells out how the release works. Hold off on buying. Have someone who knows exit hardware look at the door first, since the bar and the lock need to work as one setup.

### Do I still need to rekey if I switch to keyless entry?

On the doors the system covers, usually no. You delete the person. The leftovers are the catch: a back office, a storage closet, anything still on a mechanical lock. Rekey those so the old keys quit working there too.

### Is keyless entry worth it for a business with only one door?

Maybe. Staff coming and going, or wanting a record of who's been in? Then yes. Just you and two people you'd trust with your house? A good deadbolt does fine. Try the 3-Question Keyless Test and see where you land.

### Not Sure Which Side of the Line You're On?

Call (443) 545-2775 and tell us about your doors and your staff. Or send the details through the request form and we'll call you back. We cover Northeast Maryland & Delaware, and we'll say so if keys will do the job.

## Commercial Rekey Guide With a Simple Key Audit

Source: https://deluxelocksmiths.com/blog/commercial-rekey-decision-guide-key-audit/

By the Deluxe Locksmith team October 15, 2026

A rekey fixes who can open a door, not a worn lock. Start with a three-count key audit and the right fix follows.

A commercial rekey is the right fix when you can name a key that is out of your control and the lock itself still works well. If the hardware is worn, or if you can't say who holds which keys, a rekey alone won't solve the problem. So start with a key audit that takes a few hours and tells you whether to rekey, replace the lock, or move a door to electronic access.

Skimming? Here's the gist. Count the keys you handed out and the keys you got back, then find out which doors share a master. If any key is missing and the lock turns smoothly, rekey that door, and each door the missing key opens. If the lock sticks or wobbles, fix the hardware first. If people come and go each month, look at electronic access for the busiest door.

Key Takeaways

- A rekey changes the pins inside the cylinder so old keys stop working, while the lock hardware on the door stays in place.
- The size of a rekey depends on the highest level of key that is missing. A lost change key affects one door, and a lost master key affects all the doors under it.
- Rekeying each time someone leaves isn't always easy, but rekeying right after an unreturned key or a bad exit often is.
- ANSI/BHMA A156.28 is the industry's recommended practice for keying systems and key management (BHMA, A156.28-2023 Recommended Practices for Mechanical Keying Systems). It is a recommended practice, not a law.

On this page

- What does a key audit actually check?
- When is a commercial rekey the right fix?
- When is rekeying the wrong fix?
- Should you rekey, replace, or go electronic?
- What does a lost master key really mean?
- What should you ask a locksmith before booking?
- Frequently asked questions

What does a key audit actually check?

A key audit is a written list of each door, each key that opens it, and each person who holds one of those keys. Most small businesses have never made one, even though keys go out over the years, a few get copied, and no one writes it down.

The risk is real here, since the Maryland State Police counted 205 breaking or entering offenses in Cecil County in 2024, down from 253 in 2020, and 10,932 statewide. That total covers homes and businesses combined, so it does not separate out commercial break-ins. (Maryland State Police, 2024 Crime in Maryland, Breaking or Entering by County, page 15; data retrieved 2026-10-18.)

We call the quick version the Three-Count Key Audit, and it comes down to three numbers for each door.

- Keys issued. How many keys to this door have ever gone out? Include spares in desk drawers and the one the cleaning crew has.
- Keys back. How many of those can you put on the table today?
- Master level. Does a master or sub-master key also open this door? If yes, each holder of that master counts too.

If the first number is bigger than the second, you have a key out of your control, so write the counts down as a table that looks like this.

Door | Keys issued | Keys back | Opened by a master? | Last rekeyed | Notes

Front entrance | 6 | 5 | Yes | Unknown | Former shift lead never returned key

Back delivery door | 3 | 3 | Yes | 2025 | Vendor key returned

Office | 2 | 2 | Yes | Unknown |

Stockroom | 4 | 3 | No | Unknown | One spare missing

In this example, the front entrance and the stockroom each have a missing key, and because the front entrance is also on the master, the master holders matter too.

If your doors sit on a master system, our guide to master key systems for multi-door businesses explains how the levels fit.

When is a commercial rekey the right fix?

A commercial rekey is the right fix when the lock works and the problem is who can open it. Rekeying swaps the pins inside the cylinder for a new combination, so the old keys stop working. The handles, the lock body and the door prep all stay where they are.

Rekeying makes sense right away when:

- A key was never returned. An employee, contractor or former tenant still has one.
- Someone left on bad terms. Even if they gave the key back, they may have made a copy first.
- A master key went missing. All the doors that master opens are at risk.
- A vendor had broad access. A remodeling crew or a short-term service company no longer needs it.
- You took over a space. You don't know how many keys the last tenant handed out.

Routine rekeys are a judgment call, and your audit is a better guide than a calendar. If the counts match and no one left badly, you can often wait.

When is rekeying the wrong fix?

Rekeying changes who can open a lock, but it doesn't fix the lock. If the hardware is the real problem, a rekey just gives you new keys for a lock that is still failing.

Check for these before booking a rekey.

- The key turns hard, or only works when you jiggle it.
- The cylinder feels loose, or spins in the door.
- Does the latch catch only when someone pulls the door shut?
- Staff prop the door open because it won't close on its own.
- There was a break-in attempt.

Any of these points to commercial lock repair or a new lock first, and a door that won't close on its own is often a closer problem more than a lock problem.

Should you rekey, replace, or go electronic?

The answer depends on what your audit found, and this table covers the common cases.

What the audit found | Best fix | Why

One key missing, lock works well | Rekey that door | Fastest way to cut off the missing key

A master key missing | Rekey at the master level | All the doors under that master are at risk

Lock sticks, wobbles or was damaged | Repair or replace, then key it | A rekey won't fix worn hardware

Staff or vendors change each month | Electronic access on busy doors | Credentials can be shut off the same day

Card or code system plus a few metal keys | Disable credentials, rekey the keyed doors | Covers both ways in

Counts match, no one left badly | Wait, recheck in a few months | No key is out of your control

Electronic access deserves a closer look if turnover keeps forcing rekeys. With a card or code system, you can switch off a departing employee's credential without touching the lock. Our breakdown of whether keyless entry is worth it for a small business walks through when that pays off and when plain keys still win. Most businesses that add keyless entry systems keep at least a few keyed doors, and those still need a rekey when a key goes missing.

What does a lost master key really mean?

A lost master key is the most serious result an audit can turn up. A master opens each door beneath it in the system, and whoever finds it can open all of them.

The scope of the fix depends on the level. When a master key is lost, a locksmith often rekeys the locks at the master level and issues new master keys. Lower-level change keys may keep working, depending on how the system was designed. A locksmith needs to see the key schedule, or rebuild one, before saying which cylinders change.

Some businesses plan for this in advance, using rekeyable or interchangeable cores that let a cylinder be changed quickly without pulling the whole lock.

The bigger lesson is key control. Limit master keys to the people who truly need them, use keys that can't be copied at a hardware store, and keep the audit table current. The Maryland Community Crime Prevention Institute's commercial security survey makes the same point. It recommends that a minimum number of people hold or can access keys, and that businesses keep spare keys in a secured cabinet or vault (Maryland Community Crime Prevention Institute, Commercial/Industrial Security Survey). Our master key systems service covers designing or cleaning up a system so a single lost key causes less damage.

What should you ask a locksmith before booking?

Ask these up front so a rekey stays the size it needs to be.

- Is this a master-keyed system? If yes, ask which levels change and which keys will still work.
- Can the existing cylinders be rekeyed? Most can. Some older or high-security cylinders need parts or replacement.
- Will you check the hardware while you're there? A rekey is a good time to catch a loose cylinder or a latch that doesn't line up.
- Do you start with non-destructive methods? If keys are lost entirely, ask how the lock will be opened before anything is drilled.
- How is the job quoted? Commercial rekeys are often quoted per job, depending on the number of cylinders and the key system.

Maryland's locksmith licensing law defines rekeying as locksmith work (Maryland Code, Business Regulation § 12.5-101). Maryland's Department of Labor makes the same point about checking the provider. It advises asking each locksmith for a business street address, which shows whether they work as a mobile service, from home, or from a storefront. Ask about insurance too. The state's guidance also covers the invoice. It should show the quoted price, the type of lock serviced, the amount paid, the service address, and the locksmith's license number (Maryland Department of Labor, Maryland Locksmith Consumer Advisory).

Have your audit table ready when you call. It answers most of what a locksmith will ask.

For businesses in Elkton and across Cecil County, our commercial lock rekeying in Elkton is done on site at your building. Outside Elkton, the main commercial lock rekeying page lists each town we cover.

Frequently asked questions

How often should a business rekey its locks?

Rekey right after a key goes missing, someone leaves on bad terms, or you take over a new space. Otherwise, a current key audit is the better guide, because it shows whether any key is actually out of your control.

Can you rekey only some of the doors?

Yes, a rekey can be limited to the doors a missing key opens. On a master-keyed system, the locksmith checks which levels that key belongs to and changes only those cylinders. Doors the missing key never opened can stay as they are, along with the keys people carry now.

If a master key is lost, do all the locks need rekeying?

Often the locks under that master need to change at the master level, and the locksmith issues new master keys. Whether each individual change key also changes depends on how the system was set up. A locksmith needs to see or rebuild the key schedule before saying which cylinders are affected.

Is rekeying enough if we already use key cards?

Not always. Disabling a former employee's card or code handles the electronic doors the same day, but any door that still uses a metal key needs its own check. If someone left with a physical key to a keyed door or a key override, that door still needs a commercial rekey.

Does rekeying change how my door hardware looks?

No. A rekey changes the pins inside the cylinder, not the lever, knob, handle or trim, so the door looks the same afterward and only the keys change. Putting in new hardware is a separate job, and a locksmith can key it to the new system at the same time.

Getting the audit done

Start with the three counts, door by door. If the counts don't match, or no one knows the answers, that's the point to call.

## Locked out? Four things not to do, and one to do first

Source: https://deluxelocksmiths.com/blog/locked-out-what-not-to-do/

The damage is usually done in the short window before the locksmith is called, not by the lockout itself.

By the Deluxe Locksmith team August 15, 2026

The damage is usually done in the short window before the locksmith is called, not by the lockout itself.

### Do not force a window

If you're locked out, don't start leaning on a window, prying at the sash, or thinking one hard hit will solve it. Glass breaks in ugly ways, and even when it doesn't shatter, the damage usually spreads to the parts around it. We see bent tracks, cracked vinyl, split wood, torn screens, and latches ripped out of alignment. A lockout is one problem. A damaged window turns it into a repair job that follows you after the door is open.

The part most people don't expect is the frame damage. Once a window frame gets forced, it often never sits square again. That means drafts, water getting where it should not, and a sash that sticks or will not close the way it used to. On older homes around Elkton, especially where the frames have already seen years of swelling and settling, that damage can be permanent. People think they are saving themselves trouble by using the window. In practice, it is one of the most common ways a simple lockout becomes an insurance claim.

There is also the security issue afterward. A window that no longer locks properly is not a small detail you deal with later. If the latch is bent, the keeper pulls loose, or the frame no longer lines up, you have created a second entry point that may not be secure that night. Even if the glass is intact, a weakened frame can make the window much easier to force the next time, by you or by someone else. If you are standing outside frustrated in a driveway off Pulaski Highway, it can feel like the fastest option. It usually creates more damage than the original problem and leaves the house less secure once you get back in.

### Do not attack the lock with tools

A locked door often stays a lockout problem until someone starts digging at the keyway with a screwdriver or grabbing the cylinder with pliers. That's when it turns into lock damage. The pins, springs, plug, and face of the cylinder are small parts built to line up precisely. A screwdriver spreads the keyway, burrs the inside, and snaps off pieces that fall deeper into the lock. Pliers on the outside usually do the same kind of harm from the other direction. Instead of opening a working lock, we arrive to a lock that has been twisted, crushed, or jammed solid.

That matters because a lock that could have been opened cleanly may now have to be drilled out and replaced. Even if the door itself is fine, a chewed-up cylinder gives us less to work with. If the plug is distorted or the keyway is packed with broken metal, the non-destructive option disappears. People are usually trying to help themselves, but the force they use is exactly what takes a repairable lock and makes it unrecoverable.

It also closes off another good option after entry: rekeying. If the cylinder is still intact, we can often change the pins so the old key no longer works and issue a new key for the same hardware. That keeps the lock matched to your door and avoids changing out parts that were otherwise serviceable. Once the cylinder has been wrecked with tools, rekeying is off the table because there is no sound cylinder left to pin. If you're standing outside your home in Elkton or coming back to a storefront off Pulaski Highway, put the tools down before you make the lock itself the bigger problem.

### The card trick does not work on your door

That trick comes from a very specific kind of door: a spring latch, no deadbolt thrown, and enough slop in the fit between the door and frame to slide a flexible card in at the right angle. On that setup, the card can press the beveled latch back into the door. That's the whole idea. If your door has a deadbolt engaged, the card does nothing, because a deadbolt is a solid bar projecting into the frame. There is no spring to push back. On a tighter, better-fitted door, there usually isn't enough space to reach the latch properly anyway.

On most modern exterior doors, trying it just damages things. People end up bending the latch, chewing up the weatherstripping, cracking the card off inside the gap, or scratching the door edge and frame. Then the door still won't open, but now the latch may not move smoothly even after we get there. We see this a lot on doors with reinforced strike plates or doors that have settled a little. The card catches, twists, and forces pressure onto parts that were never meant to be used that way.

The videos are misleading because they're usually made on the easiest possible door, often already loose, already unlatched, and filmed from the best angle with several tries cut out. You don't see the failed attempts, and you usually can't tell whether the deadbolt is actually off. A quick clip makes it look universal when it's really a narrow trick for a narrow situation. If you're standing outside a house in Cecil County or near downtown Elkton with a locked exterior door, assume the card trick is more likely to waste effort and add damage than solve the problem.

### Where you wait matters more than the lock

If you're locked out beside traffic or outside a building after dark, stop thinking about the door for a second and think about where you're standing. A locked car in a parking lot is one problem. A locked car on the shoulder of Route 40 is a different problem. The risk is not the lock. It's poor visibility, distracted drivers, and being stuck in a spot where nobody can tell whether you need help. If you can move safely, get to a place that's lit, open, and easy for other people to see. That usually means near a storefront, a gas station, a lobby, or under working exterior lights, not tucked behind a dumpster or down the side of a building.

If the vehicle is in a dangerous spot, don't stand between it and traffic, and don't lean into the road trying to wave someone down. Stay well off the travel lane. If you can safely reach a safer area nearby, do that first and keep the vehicle in sight if possible. If the area feels active and public, staying near the car often makes sense because it helps us find you and helps you keep an eye on the vehicle. If the area feels isolated, badly lit, or you're outside alone late in the evening, your safety matters more than staying next to the door. Step into a nearby business or another visible public place and call from there.

The reason we give this advice is simple: lockouts turn into bigger problems when people freeze in a bad spot or stay hidden because they're embarrassed. We'd much rather have you calm, visible, and easy to locate than standing in a dark corner focused on the handle. If you call us from somewhere safer, tell us exactly where the vehicle or building entrance is and where you'll be waiting so we can meet you without confusion.

### What a locksmith will ask you to prove

Before we open anything, we need to know you have the right to be there. That is not us being difficult. It protects your property, your family, your landlord if you rent, and our technicians as well. A lockout can look the same whether it's an honest mistake or someone trying to get into a place or car that isn't theirs. Proof of entitlement is the line that keeps a stressful situation from turning into the wrong kind of call.

For a home, the simplest proof is usually a government photo ID with the same address as the house. If your ID still shows an old address, that does not automatically stop things. Mail, a utility bill, closing paperwork, or another document that ties your name to that property can help. If you're locked out of a rental, we may ask for a lease, rent portal information, or for the property manager or landlord to confirm that you live there. That protects tenants too. It helps make sure a former roommate, ex, or unauthorized guest is not using a locksmith to get past the door.

For a vehicle, registration, insurance, or title with your name on it is usually what we're looking for, along with photo ID. If those papers are inside the car, tell us that up front. That's common, and we can usually verify once the vehicle is open. If the car is a company vehicle, a work ID or a call from the business may be needed. None of this is an obstacle put in your way. It's normal, responsible practice. If you can, have your ID and any paperwork ready while you wait, whether you're at home in Elkton or parked off Pulaski Highway. It makes the job smoother and keeps the right person on the right side of the lock.

### What non-destructive entry actually means

Most lockouts do not require breaking anything. The job is to get the door open and leave the lock, the door, and the frame working the same way they did before you were shut out. That matters because a lock is only one part of the opening. If the latch gets bent, the strike gets torn loose, or the frame gets spread, you can end up with a door that closes badly, drags, or will not secure properly even after the key is back in your hand. Non-destructive entry means we start with methods meant to defeat the lock or the latch without damaging the hardware around it.

Why that works so often is simple: most lockouts are access problems, not broken-door problems. A key is inside, a knob got locked, a deadbolt was thrown, or the latch shut behind you. If the lock is in decent shape, there is usually a clean way in. We check what type of cylinder or latch you have, how the door is handing, and whether the hardware is aligned normally. A front door in Elkton that was working fine before the lockout should, in most cases, work fine after we open it.

There are exceptions, and it is better to be straight about them. Some high-security cylinders are designed to resist the usual opening methods. In other cases, the lock was already failing, packed with debris, misaligned, or partly damaged from prior force. Then the cleanest option can be to sacrifice the cylinder to protect the rest of the door. That means the removable core of the lock is drilled or otherwise taken out so the door can be opened without wrecking the door slab or frame. After that, we replace the cylinder or the affected lock hardware, test the latch and deadbolt, and make sure the door locks and unlocks correctly before we leave.

### The lockout scam to watch for

One pattern shows up over and over in lockouts. The person on the phone gives a neat, reassuring quote before they've asked the basic questions that matter: what kind of door, what kind of lock, whether the key is inside, whether anything is broken already. Then an unmarked vehicle pulls up, not a van or car that clearly belongs to a locksmith business. Once they're at the door, the number changes and the answer to everything is, "We have to drill it." That is the part to watch. Drilling is fast for the wrong operator because it turns a simple opening into a lock replacement, and that shifts the job in their favor, not yours.

A legitimate locksmith works the other way around. We ask enough over the phone to understand what we're coming to, because the door and hardware tell us a lot about the likely entry method. When we arrive, we identify who we are and look at the lock before touching it. If a lock can be opened without destroying it, that is usually the first route. Drilling is a last resort, not the opening move, because once metal is cut there is no undo button. You're no longer dealing with a lockout alone; now you're dealing with parts, rekeying, and a door that may not secure properly until the whole job is finished.

The reason this scam works is simple: most people are stressed and standing outside their own door, whether that's at a townhouse off Pulaski Highway or a storefront in Elkton. Stress makes vague answers sound good enough. Slow the process down just enough to ask direct questions: What are you driving, what company are you with, and why do you believe drilling is necessary on this specific lock. A real locksmith can answer that plainly.

### After the door is open

Getting back inside solves the immediate problem, but it doesn't always solve the reason it happened. A lockout is often a warning. If your keys were lost or taken, the smart move is to have the lock re-coded on the same visit. That changes the lock to work with a different key, so the missing key no longer fits. People sometimes put that off because the door is open and life moves on. Then the lost key turns up in the wrong hands, or it stays out there and nags at you every time you leave the house.

The same goes for a lock or door that was already giving you trouble. If you had to jiggle the key, lift the handle, shove the door, or pull it just right before this happened, that problem did not fix itself. It will usually do the same thing again, and often at the worst time. In a lot of homes around Cecil County, the lock gets blamed when the real issue is alignment: the latch isn't meeting the strike cleanly, the deadbolt is binding, or the door has shifted enough that everything feels stiff. Forcing it every day wears the key, the cylinder, and the hardware around it.

That's why we tell people to use the open door as a chance to sort the root cause while we're there. If the lock is worn, we can tell you whether it needs service or replacement. If the strike needs adjustment, the cylinder is loose, the key is badly copied, or the closer is pulling the door out of position, those are worth fixing before you lock up again. The goal is not just to get you in. It's to leave you with a door that works cleanly the next time you step out, whether you're in Elkton or heading home after a stop off Route 40.

## Master Key Systems for Multi-Door Businesses

Source: https://deluxelocksmiths.com/blog/master-key-systems-what-multi-door-businesses-actually-need/

By the Deluxe Locksmith team September 17, 2026

A master key system lets one key open every door in a building. Individual keys still work on their own doors only. That's the short version. The longer version is where most businesses get it wrong. Some install more than they need. Others stick with a pile of individual keys long after the building outgrew that approach.

Skimming? Here's the gist. More than a handful of interior doors? Staff turnover, or more than one person needing different room combinations? A tiered master key system is usually worth it. A single office with two doors and the same three people for years? It usually isn't. Deluxe Locksmith installs and services master key systems across Cecil County, Maryland, including Elkton, North East, Rising Sun, and Perryville.

### What Does a Master Key System Actually Do?

A master key system uses a tiered set of cylinders. One master key opens every door. Sub-master keys open groups of doors. Individual change keys open only their assigned door. In 2026, that structure fits most commercial properties with more than 4-5 interior doors and multiple staff roles. It beats a copy of every key for every person.

The point isn't convenience for convenience's sake. It's separation. A manager might need the office, the stock room, and the front door. A part-time employee might only need the front door. Without tiering, giving that manager the right access usually means giving everyone the same access. Cutting individual keys for every combination gets unmanageable fast.

People tend to think of master keying as an all-or-nothing upgrade. It isn't. A two-level setup, one master plus a handful of change keys, solves the problem for a small office. A three- or four-level structure with sub-masters by department fits better on a property with distinct zones. Think a warehouse with an office, a loading area, and a secured inventory room. Match the tiering to how the building actually gets used, not the other way around.

#### Master Key vs. Rekeying: Different Problems

Rekeying and master keying get confused often. Mixing them up wastes money. Rekeying changes the pins in an existing lock, so old keys stop working. It's useful after a lost key or an employee departure. A master key system is different: a structural decision about who can open what, built once and adjusted as roles change.

If your business just needs old keys deactivated after someone leaves, that's commercial lock rekeying, not a new plan. If you're constantly juggling who has which key and the answer keeps getting messier, that's the sign you need a tiered structure.

#### Restricted Keyways and the Cross-Keying Trap

Standard keyways can be duplicated at any hardware store or kiosk. A restricted keyway uses a patent-protected key blank that only a licensed locksmith can cut, which closes off the easiest way an unauthorized copy gets made. For a master key system, that matters more than it does for a single lock: one uncontrolled copy of a master doesn't just open one door, it opens all of them.

There's a failure mode worth knowing about too: cross-keying. It happens when a system gets stretched past its original design, usually one exception at a time. A manager needs access to a room outside their normal level, so a tech pins a workaround instead of restructuring the hierarchy. Do that enough times over a few years and the master key stops meaning what it's supposed to mean. Anyone who's inherited a messy key system knows the sign: nobody can explain anymore why a certain key opens a certain door. The fix is a proper re-master, not another one-off exception. If a system already feels like that, treat it as a sign the structure needs rebuilding, not patching again.

### Why Does Key Control Matter for a Multi-Door Business?

U.S. voluntary employee turnover averaged 13% in 2025, down from 24.7% in 2022 (Mercer's 2025 US Turnover Survey, 2025). Still meaningful for any business with more than a few employees. Every departure without a clear rekey policy leaves a key in circulation that nobody is tracking anymore.

We see this most often with businesses that have been in the same location for years. Nobody remembers exactly how many keys were cut. Nobody's sure who still has one, or whether a contractor from three years ago ever returned theirs. By the time someone asks the question, the honest answer is usually "we don't know." That's precisely the situation documented key control prevents.

A properly set up system comes with a schedule: a written record of which key level opens which doors, and who was issued one. That record is what makes it possible to answer "who can get into the server room" without guessing.

### When Is a Master Key System Overkill?

A master key system is overkill for a small building. Think one or two doors, a small stable staff, no meaningful separation needed between roles. If everyone already needs access to everything, tiering just adds paperwork without solving a real problem.

The FBI recorded 779,542 burglaries nationwide in 2024, the lowest count in decades (Crime in the United States, FBI, 2024 data). Residential properties made up roughly 52% of that total, so commercial properties account for close to half. That risk exists regardless of building size. But the response to it should scale with the building. A single-office business is usually better served by solid commercial lock hardware and a straightforward rekey policy than by a multi-tier setup it doesn't need.

### How Do You Know Which Level of System Fits Your Business?

The right level depends on how many distinct access groups exist, not how many doors there are. A five-door building with one access group, everyone can go everywhere, needs a simple setup. A three-door building with a manager, hourly staff, and a cleaning contractor needing different combinations needs tiering anyway, even with fewer doors.

Start by listing who needs access to what. Go role by role, not door by door. Once that list exists, the number of key levels usually becomes obvious. It's also worth asking whether every space needs its own physical key. An electronic point might make more sense for one or two high-traffic doors, while the rest stay on a traditional setup.

#### A Simple Way to Think About It

Business situation

Likely fit

1-2 doors, small stable staff, everyone needs the same access

Standard keying, no master system

3-6 doors, a few access groups (manager, staff, contractor)

Two- or three-level master system

7+ doors, multiple departments, frequent staff changes

Multi-level master system with a documented key schedule

High-traffic single entry needing audit trail

Consider electronic access for that door, keyed master for the rest

#### What About Businesses With More Than One Location?

A business running two or three sites usually wants two things that pull in opposite directions: a manager who can move between locations without carrying separate rings, and a guarantee that a key from one site can't open doors at another. A grand master key structure handles both. Each location keeps its own master level, and one grand master sits above all of them for whoever needs cross-site access. The key schedule just needs an extra column for location, not a whole separate system per site.

#### Master Keying and Life-Safety Hardware

Master keying doesn't happen in isolation from the rest of a door's hardware. Exit routes on commercial buildings often need panic bar hardware to meet code, and a poorly matched cylinder can interfere with how that hardware latches and releases. Anyone setting up a master system on a building with panic-hardware exits should have both pieces looked at together, not as two separate jobs scheduled months apart.

### Frequently Asked Questions

#### Can a master key system be added to locks I already have?

Often, yes. Many commercial cylinders can be re-pinned to fit a new tiered structure without replacing the entire lock body. That keeps the work focused on the pins and keying. No tearing out hardware that still works (The Benefits of a Master Key System in a Commercial Building, HOPPE, accessed 2026).

#### What happens if a master key gets lost?

That's a real problem, because a lost master can open every door under it, not just one. The fix is usually rekeying every lock under that master to a fresh keying. That's exactly why access to masters should stay limited to the smallest group of people who genuinely need it.

#### How is a master key system different from an electronic access system?

A master key setup is entirely physical: no batteries, no software, no network dependency. An electronic system adds audit trails and remote deactivation, but depends on power and software to keep working. Many multi-door businesses use both, electronic access on one or two high-traffic doors, a physical master system for the rest.

#### Do I need a master key system if I only have three employees?

Not necessarily. If all three need the same access and the building has one or two doors, a standard rekey after any departure usually covers the risk. A tiered structure earns its place once access actually needs to differ by role.

### Getting a System Set Up

Not sure whether your building needs a two-level setup or something more layered? The starting point is the same either way: a walk-through of the doors, the roles, and who currently has keys to what. Deluxe Locksmith handles that assessment on-site across Elkton and the rest of Cecil County. Then it's a schedule: a written record of who can open what.

On-site, that usually means counting doors, checking what's already installed, and asking who needs into which spaces. Have a rough headcount and department breakdown ready. It speeds things up. For a straightforward two- or three-level setup, most of that assessment happens in a single visit. A larger, multi-department property might need a second pass to get the grouping right before any cylinders get pinned.

A key schedule isn't a one-time document either. Staff change, departments get added, and a level that made sense two years ago might not fit the business today. Worth a quick review any time roles shift significantly, not just when a key goes missing.

## Does Your Cecil County Business Need a Panic Bar?

Source: https://deluxelocksmiths.com/blog/panic-bar-installation-code-compliance-cecil-county-businesses/

Panic hardware is required on most commercial exits with 50 or more occupants. Here is the code, the common mistakes, and when to call a pro.

By the Deluxe Locksmith team September 24, 2026

Panic hardware is required on most commercial exits with 50 or more occupants. Here is the code, the common mistakes, and when to call a pro.

A panic bar is the bar people push to get out, and that makes it a life-safety item first and a piece of hardware second. Most Cecil County business owners assume any push bar satisfies the code. It usually doesn't. The requirements are specific, and the mistakes we see on service calls are consistent enough to be worth walking through before an inspector finds them for you.

Skimming? Here's the gist. Exit doors serving 50 or more occupants generally need panic hardware under the International Building Code. Mounting height, the fire-rated vs. standard hardware distinction, and how panic bars interact with keyless entry are the three places businesses most often get it wrong. Deluxe Locksmith installs and corrects panic hardware across Cecil County, Maryland, including Elkton, North East, and Rising Sun.

### Does Your Business Need a Panic Bar?

In 2026, the International Building Code requires panic hardware on exit doors serving Assembly or Educational occupancies with a calculated occupant load of 50 or more (IBC 2024, Chapter 10, Means of Egress, International Code Council, 2024). Some spaces need it regardless of occupant load, including transformer vaults, battery and energy storage rooms, and modular data centers. That covers a surprising number of Cecil County storefronts, restaurants, and offices once you actually run the headcount.

Easy to miss: the 2024 IBC also requires panic hardware on any exit door within 25 feet of electrical equipment rated 800 amps or more, such as a main electrical room or switchgear closet, regardless of the room's occupant load (Decoded: Which doors need panic hardware?, I Dig Hardware, Allegion, 2026). Businesses with a back-of-house electrical or utility room rarely think to check this one, since it has nothing to do with staff or customer headcount. Deluxe Locksmith can check your utility and electrical rooms during the same visit as the rest of your exits, so this kind of code gap doesn't get missed until an inspector catches it.

Maryland enforces these requirements through the Office of the State Fire Marshal, operating under the Maryland Department of State Police, using the state's adopted fire prevention code (State of Maryland Fire Prevention Code, Maryland State Fire Marshal, 2024). The office has broad authority to inspect buildings and penalize violations. If you're not sure whether your building crosses the 50-occupant threshold, that's worth confirming before you assume a standard commercial lock is enough.

A retail space with two or three staff and light foot traffic might stay under the threshold. A restaurant, a fitness studio, or a multi-tenant office building rarely does once customers, staff, and peak hours are counted together. If your occupancy classification or headcount is close to the line, treat it as a question for your local fire marshal's office, not a guess.

### What Actually Counts as Panic Hardware?

Panic hardware lets a door open with a single motion under simple pressure, normally latched until someone pushes the bar. A rim panic bar, where the latch mechanism sits in a case mounted on the interior door face, is the most common configuration for a retrofit because it suits most wood and hollow-metal doors without major modification (How to Install a Panic Bar, National Lock Supply, accessed 2026).

Two numbers matter more than any others. Panic hardware mounts 34 to 48 inches above the floor or threshold, and the touchpad or crossbar spans at least half the width of the door leaf (IBC Requirements for Panic Bars, Automatic Door and Hardware, accessed 2026). Both specs stay consistent across code authorities and installer guides, which is why they're the two things worth remembering even if you forget everything else in this post.

### What Is the Difference Between Panic Hardware and Fire Exit Hardware?

Standard panic hardware often includes a dogging feature that lets staff hold the latch retracted during business hours, useful on a busy retail entrance. Fire-rated doors prohibit that entirely. They require UL-listed fire exit hardware that stays latched at all times, so the door can contain smoke and flame if a fire breaks out on the other side (Code Requirements for Panic Door Hardware in 2026, Vortex Doors, 2026). A business that dogs a fire-rated door for convenience isn't just breaking a rule. It's defeating the reason that door has a fire rating in the first place.

#### A Simple Way to Tell Them Apart

Feature

Standard panic hardware

Fire exit hardware

Dogging (latch held retracted)

Often allowed

Never allowed

Fire rating

Not required

UL-listed, required on fire-rated doors

Typical use

Standard exit doors, no fire rating

Fire-rated corridor and stairwell doors

Common mistake

Used where fire exit hardware belongs

Rare to see the reverse

This distinction is easy to miss because both types look nearly identical from across a room. It only becomes obvious once someone checks the door's fire rating against the hardware actually installed on it, which is exactly the kind of thing a panic bar installation assessment is meant to catch.

### What Is the Keyless Entry Trap Most Businesses Don't Know About?

As of the 2024 IBC, a door required to have panic hardware can no longer have its electromagnetic lock released by a motion sensor alone. Release has to come from a switch built into the panic hardware itself, along with a loss-of-power release (What's Next? Approved changes to the 2024 IBC affecting electrified hardware, I Dig Hardware, Allegion, 2022). That rule directly affects any Cecil County business considering keyless entry on an exit door, and it's not something most badge-reader vendors bring up during the sales pitch.

If you're weighing keyless entry for convenience or an audit trail, plan the panic hardware and the access control as one project, not two. A system installed in the wrong order, or by an installer who only handles one side of it, is where this mistake usually happens. Our guide on whether keyless entry is worth it for a small business covers how to choose a credential and what to check before you buy.

### What We Commonly Find on Service Calls

Dogged fire-rated doors are the most frequent issue: a latch held retracted for staff convenience on a door that legally can't allow it. Wrong mounting height comes next, usually from a previous DIY install or a general contractor who treated the panic bar like any other hardware line item. Incompatible strikes and closers show up too, where the panic hardware and the rest of the door's hardware were never matched to work together.

None of these are dramatic on their own. Together, they're why panic hardware that looks fine from across the room can still fail an inspection, and why a walk-through by someone who installs this hardware regularly catches problems a quick visual check won't.

### Why Professional Installation Matters

Door and frame compatibility, correct hardware grade, and code-compliant mounting all have to line up for panic hardware to pass inspection. NFPA 101 requires panic hardware to be listed to ANSI/BHMA A156.3, the exit device standard (Decoded: Which doors need panic hardware?, I Dig Hardware, Allegion, 2026), and the device still has to be installed from the manufacturer's template and tested so the latch releases from anywhere along the touchpad (How to Install a Panic Bar, National Lock Supply, accessed 2026). That's the consensus among installers who work on this hardware regularly, echoed in a trade discussion among commercial door contractors weighing panic bar options for their own jobs.

This is one of the few pieces of commercial hardware where a good-enough install isn't actually good enough. The door either releases correctly under code-required conditions or it doesn't, and an inspector isn't grading on effort.

### Frequently Asked Questions

#### Does my business need a panic bar?

Usually yes if an exit door serves an assembly or educational occupancy with a calculated occupant load of 50 or more, per the International Building Code. Some rooms, like electrical vaults and battery storage, need panic hardware regardless of occupant load. Maryland enforces this through the Office of the State Fire Marshal, so a local inspection is the final word for your specific building.

#### What's the difference between panic hardware and fire exit hardware?

Standard panic hardware often has a dogging feature that holds the latch retracted during business hours. Fire-rated doors prohibit that. They require UL-listed fire exit hardware that stays latched so the door can contain smoke and flame during a fire. Installing the wrong one on a fire-rated door is a compliance failure, not a cosmetic mismatch.

#### How high should a panic bar be mounted?

Panic hardware is typically mounted 34 to 48 inches above the floor or threshold, and the touchpad or crossbar needs to span at least half the width of the door leaf. Those numbers stay consistent across code authorities and installer guides, which is why they're the two specs worth memorizing.

#### Can I add a keypad or badge reader to a door with a panic bar?

Yes, but the 2024 IBC changed how it has to work. A door required to have panic hardware can no longer have its electromagnetic lock released by a motion sensor alone. Release has to come from a switch built into the panic hardware itself, plus a loss-of-power release. That matters for any business adding keyless entry to an exit door.

#### Do panic bars need to be inspected?

Panic hardware on required exits typically falls under fire code inspection, since it's classified as life-safety equipment rather than ordinary door hardware. Inspection frequency and specifics vary by jurisdiction and occupancy type, so check with your local fire marshal's office for the exact schedule that applies to your building.

### Getting Your Panic Hardware Checked

Not sure whether your current setup would pass inspection? The starting point is the same either way: a walk-through of the exit doors, their occupancy classification, and what hardware is currently installed. Deluxe Locksmith handles that assessment on-site across Elkton and the rest of Cecil County. If a door needs correcting, that's addressed on the same visit whenever possible.

Have your building's occupancy type and a rough headcount ready before the visit. It speeds up the walk-through. If you're also planning keyless entry on any exit door, mention that up front so the panic hardware and access control get planned together instead of as two separate jobs.

## Rekey or replace? How to tell which one you need

Source: https://deluxelocksmiths.com/blog/rekey-or-replace-your-locks/

Two different problems with two different answers, and people routinely pay for the wrong one.

By the Deluxe Locksmith team August 17, 2026

Two different problems with two different answers, and people routinely pay for the wrong one.

### Rekey when the hardware is fine and the keys are the problem

Most of the time, the lock itself is not the problem. The key history is. That's what rekeying is for. If you bought a house, took over a rental, had staff turnover, lost a key, ended a relationship, or gave a contractor a key that never made its way back, the question is simple: do you still trust every copy that might be out there? If the lock works smoothly and the door is securing the way it should, changing the keying is usually the right move. You're not fixing broken hardware. You're cutting off old access.

This is the most common situation by a wide margin. People often assume they need all new locks after a move, but the real issue is that they have no way to know who still has a working key. The seller may have handed over two copies, but there could be extras with a neighbor, a dog walker, a former roommate, or a family member. Same idea at a business after an employee leaves. If one person had a key and you can't account for every copy, you have a security problem even if the lock is working perfectly.

We see the same thing after a breakup or after repair work on a house. Nobody wants to accuse anybody of bad intentions, but security is not about guessing people's motives. It's about control. Rekeying resets that control so the old keys stop working and only the new keys do. If you're in Cecil County and you just closed on a house, or a storefront off Pulaski Highway changed hands, this is usually the first lock decision to make. Not because the lock failed, but because the trust attached to the old key is gone.

### Replace when the hardware itself is the problem

If the lock itself is worn out, damaged, or wrong for the job, rekeying won't solve the real problem. Rekeying only changes which key operates the cylinder. It does not repair sloppy internal parts, a weak latch, a cracked tailpiece, a bent bolt, or corrosion that's already eating into the mechanism. If the hardware is failing mechanically, the right answer is replacement, because the problem is no longer key control. It's reliability and security.

The signs are usually pretty clear once you know what to look for. If the key has to be jiggled every time, if it sticks going in or coming out, if the lock turns roughly even with a good key, or if the deadbolt only throws when you push, pull, or lift the door, something is wearing out or out of alignment. Rust around the cylinder, a faceplate that's loose, a latch that doesn't spring back cleanly, or a deadbolt that drags are all signs the hardware is past the point where a pin change helps. We also see locks that were fine years ago but are now the wrong grade for the traffic they get. A light-duty knob lock on a busy side door in Elkton or a storefront entrance near Route 40 may technically still work, but it wears fast because it was never meant for that use.

Replacement is also the right move when the type of lock no longer fits what you need. Maybe you need a proper deadbolt instead of relying on a keyed knob, panic hardware instead of a standard lever, or a weather-rated lock because corrosion keeps coming back. In those cases, keeping the old hardware and rekeying it just preserves the mismatch. We look at how the lock is built, how the door closes, and how the opening is actually used, because a lock should fit the door and the job, not just accept a new key.

### How rekeying actually works

Rekeying changes the lock's working combination without changing the lock you see on the door. We take the cylinder out of the knob, lever, or deadbolt and open it up on the bench. Inside that cylinder is a stack of small pins that line up to one specific key cut. We replace or rearrange those pins so the old key no longer lines them up, then we cut a new key to match the new pin pattern. After that, the cylinder goes back into the same lock body and the lock works like it always did, just with a different key.

That's why rekeying leaves the visible hardware alone. The trim, finish, and shape on the door stay the same because we are not swapping the whole deadbolt or knob set. If your satin nickel hardware matches the rest of the house, or your storefront hardware is mounted and working properly, there is no reason to disturb it just to stop an old key from working. The change happens in the part that reads the key, not in the parts you grab with your hand.

It is also quicker than full replacement because there is less to take apart and less to fit back onto the door. A replacement means removing the existing hardware, making sure the new parts match the door prep, latch backset, strike alignment, and screw spacing, then testing all of it together. With a rekey, the door usually keeps the same hardware and the same fit. We are changing the lock's internal code, not rebuilding the door. For a lot of homes and businesses around Elkton and up toward Route 40, that is the right fix when the issue is the key access, not the lock itself.

### How many times can a lock be rekeyed

There isn't a set number. A good lock cylinder can be rekeyed over and over as long as the core parts are still in solid shape. Rekeying changes the pin setup inside the plug so a different key works. That process doesn't automatically "use up" a lock. What matters is the condition of the plug, the keyway, and the small parts that have to move cleanly every time you turn the key. If those surfaces are still sound, we can usually rekey it again.

What actually wears out is metal. Keys rubbing in the keyway over the years can round things off. The plug can get sloppy inside the cylinder. Pins and springs can wear, stick, or stop lining up the way they should. Dirt, old lubricant, weather, and a badly worn key all speed that up. That's why two locks of the same age can be very different: one may still rekey nicely, while the other has enough internal wear that changing the pins won't fix the real problem.

The signs are pretty practical. If the key has to be jiggled just right, if turning feels rough even with the correct key, if the plug has noticeable play, or if the key goes in and out loosely, the cylinder may be nearing the end of what rekeying can solve. Another red flag is a lock that still acts up after it's cleaned and a proper key is cut. At that point the issue usually isn't the key combination anymore; it's wear in the hardware itself.

That's why we inspect the cylinder before recommending anything, whether we're at a house off Pulaski Highway or a storefront near downtown Elkton. People often ask, "Can this be rekeyed again?" The honest answer is yes, many times, until the lock starts showing wear that affects how it operates. Then replacement becomes the reliable fix, not because of a number, but because the metal has had enough.

### Getting several locks onto one key

If you're tired of carrying one key for the front door, another for the side door, and a third for the deadbolt in the garage entry, we can often set those locks up so one key works across the house. That's called keyed alike. It's practical because you stop guessing which key goes where, and it cuts down on the extra copies floating around on keyrings, in junk drawers, and with relatives or dog walkers. For a normal home setup, this works best when the locks are the same brand and use the same keyway, which is the shape of the keyway slot and the matching key blank.

This is where people get tripped up. Two locks can look similar on the door and still not be able to take the same key. If one lock is Kwikset and the other is Schlage, they usually won't key alike because the internal parts and keyways are different. Even within one manufacturer, some product lines use different keyways, so one Schlage key may not fit another Schlage lock. If you've got a mix of old hardware, builder-grade knobs, and a newer deadbolt added later, we check what's actually there before saying yes. Sometimes the answer is simple rekeying. Sometimes one lock has to be replaced if your goal is one key across everything.

There's also a real security trade-off, and it's worth saying plainly. One key for every exterior door is convenient, but if that one key is lost, stolen, or copied without your knowledge, it opens every lock in that keyed-alike group. With separate keys, a lost key may only affect one door. Some households are fine with that trade because daily use matters more. Others would rather keep a detached garage, rental space, or back entry on a different key. Around Elkton and out toward Route 40, we usually tell people to think about who has copies, not just how handy one-key access sounds.

### Restricted keys, and who can copy your key

If your key is a standard house or office key, anyone holding it can usually get a copy made at a hardware store or kiosk. The machine does not know whether that person is the owner, a tenant, an employee, or someone who borrowed the key for an afternoon. It just reads the cuts and duplicates them. That matters because a lot of people think rekeying alone controls copies. It does not. Rekeying changes which key works the lock. It does not stop that new key from being copied if it is an ordinary keyway.

A restricted keyway is different. Those keys and blanks are controlled, so duplication is limited to authorized holders through the locksmith or system owner. The point is not that the key is magical. The point is control. If you manage rentals, employee access, maintenance staff, cleaners, or a shared building with several people carrying keys, restricted keys give you a real chain of permission. You know who is allowed to order more keys, and random copies are much harder to make. For a property manager with units off Pulaski Highway, or a business with staff turnover, that solves a problem ordinary keys do not.

A lot of homeowners do not need that level of control. If it is your own house, only a couple of family members have keys, and you are not handing them out to contractors or rotating occupants, a standard key is often fine. Restricted keys make sense when key copies themselves are the risk. They are not automatically better for every front door in Elkton. The right question is simple: are you trying to control who can open the lock, or who can create more keys. Those are two different problems, and they need different answers.

### Grades, and what they actually mean for your door

A lock grade is basically a shorthand for how much use and abuse a lock is built to take, and how well it stands up when someone tries to force it. That matters, but it gets oversold. A better grade does not turn every lock into a fortress, and it does not mean every door in the house needs the toughest hardware made. What it should tell you is whether the lock fits the job. For a front door that gets used all day, faces weather, and is the main point of entry, you want hardware meant for repeated use and solid resistance. For a bedroom, pantry, or hall closet, that would be overkill because the job is privacy or simple latching, not exterior security.

The reason this matters is that people often buy based on the package instead of the door. A strong lock on a weak door frame is not a strong setup. On the other hand, putting light-duty hardware on a front entry that gets slammed, tugged, and used constantly is asking for early wear. If your exterior door is on a busy entrance off Pulaski Highway, it needs more from the lock than an interior office door does. Good hardware should match the traffic, the exposure, and the consequences if it fails.

What should you ask for? Ask whether the lock is suited for exterior use, whether it is built for heavy daily cycling, and whether the deadbolt and latch have solid metal parts instead of the light stuff that wears out fast. Ask whether your strike plate and screws are part of the security picture, because they are. And ask us to look at the whole door, not just the cylinder. The right answer is not always the highest grade on the shelf. It is the grade that makes sense for that specific door and how you actually use it.

### When it is a business, think in systems not locks

On a business door, the real question usually isn't "Is this lock bad?" It's "Who should be able to get into which areas, and what changes when staffing changes?" A storefront, office, warehouse, or medical space often has a front door, interior offices, storage rooms, back entries, and maybe a gate or equipment room. Not everyone should have the same access to all of it. If you treat each cylinder like a separate problem, you end up with a ring full of keys, doors nobody is fully tracking, and a lot of confusion the first time an employee leaves or a manager changes.

That is where a master key system makes sense. Instead of thinking one door at a time, we map access by role. A front desk employee may need the main entry and supply closet. A supervisor may need those plus office doors. Ownership may need one master key that opens the whole site. The point is control. You can give people the access they need to do their job without handing out a key that opens everything. That matters even more in a multi-tenant building, a shop off Pulaski Highway, or any place where deliveries, shift changes, and shared spaces are part of the day.

Staff turnover is usually what exposes a bad key setup. If someone leaves and nobody is sure which doors their key opens, you do not have a lock problem first. You have a key control problem. A planned system gives you a clear answer: this person had access to these areas, and now that access needs to be changed. That is why commercial work should start with a simple access plan, not a pile of duplicate keys. We help businesses in places like Elkton set that up so the hardware supports the way the business actually runs, instead of fighting it.
