## Smart locks: what actually matters when you buy one

Source: https://deluxelocksmiths.com/blog/smart-locks-what-actually-matters/

The app is the least important part. The mechanical fit decides whether you like it.

By the Deluxe Locksmith team August 13, 2026

The app is the least important part. The mechanical fit decides whether you like it.

### A smart lock is still a lock

Before the app, the keypad, or the brand name, the lock has to fit the door correctly. That starts with the bore hole and the backset. If the hole size is off, or the backset doesn't match the lock body, the hardware sits wrong from the start. On some doors, the lock can be made to mount, but it binds just enough to cause trouble later. A regular deadbolt might still limp along because your hand can muscle it through. A smart lock's motor can't do that. It expects the parts to line up and move cleanly every time.

The strike matters just as much. The bolt should slide into the strike opening fully, without rubbing the edge, lifting the door, or needing you to push, pull, or twist the knob to help it. If you have to lean on the door to lock it, that's not a smart-lock problem. That's an alignment problem between the door, the frame, and the strike. We see this a lot on doors that have settled, doors that swell in damp weather, and doors where the old deadbolt "worked" only because the user had gotten used to forcing it.

That's why people often install a smart lock, then decide the electronics are unreliable. The motor stalls, the lock beeps, or it says locked when the bolt didn't throw all the way. What's really happening is mechanical resistance. The lock is trying to do a deadbolt's job on a door that was already fighting the deadbolt. Around Cecil County and up near Route 40, a lot of that comes down to older doors, seasonal movement, and strike plates that were never set quite right. If the bolt can't extend smoothly by hand first, adding electronics won't fix it. It usually exposes the problem.

### Check the door before you check the reviews

A smart lock can only work with the door it's bolted to. If your current deadbolt already needs a shoulder bump, a hard twist, or a shove on the door to lock, that's the problem to solve first. The motor inside a smart lock has nowhere near the force your hand and wrist do. You can muscle a sticky deadbolt into place and barely notice it. The lock's motor can't. That's why people end up saying a smart lock is unreliable when the real issue is a door that's slightly out of alignment.

You can test this yourself before you buy anything. Open the door and throw the deadbolt in and out a few times. It should move smoothly, with no scraping, catching, or extra effort. Then do the same test with the door closed. Pay attention to the difference. If it turns easily with the door open but gets tight when the door is shut, the bolt and strike aren't lining up cleanly. That means the lock is pushing the bolt against the edge of the hole or rubbing the frame instead of sliding straight in.

That small bit of drag matters more than app features or star ratings. A smart lock is doing the same job over and over with limited battery power and a small motor. If the bolt has to fight the frame each time, you get failed locks, partial locks, fast battery drain, and the kind of behavior people call "glitchy." In a place that sees humidity swings like Cecil County, doors move a little through the year, so a setup that is barely working now usually gets worse, not better.

If the test shows resistance, fix the fit first. Sometimes that means adjusting the strike, tightening loose hardware, correcting sag at the hinges, or dealing with weatherstrip pressure. Once the deadbolt works smoothly with the door closed, a smart lock has a fair shot at working the way it should.

### Keyed override matters more than people think

Dead batteries almost never happen at a convenient time. It's usually late, your hands are full, the weather is bad, or the lock has been giving a low-battery warning that got ignored for a while. That's why we tell people not to get distracted by the app and forget the backup plan. A smart lock that still has a real key cylinder gives you a simple way in when the electronics quit. If there's no key override, the next best thing is external contacts on the outside of the lock so you can touch a battery to it long enough to wake it up and unlock the door.

That matters because a dead battery should be an annoyance, not a lockout. With a keyed override, the lock can fail in one system without trapping you outside. The mechanical side still works, and that separation is valuable. It also helps if the keypad acts up, the touchscreen stops responding in cold weather, or the lock loses power faster than expected. We see plenty of doors around Elkton where the owner assumed "battery powered" meant "problem free" until the first bad day proved otherwise.

The trade-off with keypad-only designs is mostly about convenience and appearance. Some people like the cleaner look, and some prefer not to carry a house key at all. But that cleaner look usually means you're trusting one system to do everything. If the battery dies and there's no external jump option, your only plan is hoping another entrance is open or calling for help. That's fine on paper and frustrating in real life, especially if the only door you use is the front one off Pulaski Highway.

If you want fewer surprises, pick a model with a physical key override first. If you don't want a key cylinder, make sure the lock has external emergency power contacts and that you know how they work before you need them.

### Batteries, cold and the real-world lifespan

Most smart-lock battery problems come from three things: the motor turning the lock, the radio waking up to talk, and the cold. The motor is the heavy draw. Every lock and unlock takes a burst of power to move the bolt or clutch. If the door is a little tight, or the bolt rubs because the alignment is off, the motor has to work harder every cycle and the batteries go faster. The radio matters too. Bluetooth usually sips power. Wi-Fi uses more because the lock has to reach farther and check in more often. A lock that's constantly reconnecting because of weak signal can burn through batteries a lot quicker than the same lock on a stable setup.

Winter changes the whole picture, especially on an exterior door. Batteries don't like cold, and a lock on a front door sees that temperature swing every day. A set of cells that seems fine indoors can act weak outside once the air turns cold off the Chesapeake. You'll notice it first as a slower motor, a delayed response, or a lock that works fine in the afternoon and struggles early in the morning. Cold also makes any sticky door or stiff weatherstripping more obvious, so the lock needs more force right when the batteries can deliver less.

Don't ignore a low-battery warning. Smart locks usually give notice before they quit, but they don't all fail gracefully. Some keep enough power for a few more cycles, then suddenly won't motor at all. That's why we tell people to replace the batteries as soon as the warning shows up, not after the weekend or after one more trip out through Route 40 wind and cold. Keep the exact battery type your lock calls for in the house, and use good fresh cells from the same brand and batch. Mixing old and new batteries, or using the wrong chemistry, is asking for flaky behavior that looks like a lock problem but is really a power problem.

### Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and hubs, in plain English

Bluetooth is the simple version. Your phone talks to the lock when you're standing at the door or close by. That usually means better battery life, because the lock is not trying to stay connected to your home network all day. It also means less to set up. If what you want is keyless entry, phone unlock, and maybe codes for family, Bluetooth often does the job without adding much complexity. The tradeoff is reach. If you're at work, away for the weekend, or just upstairs and out of range, you usually can't check the lock or change anything until you're back near it.

Wi-Fi is the opposite. It lets the lock talk through your internet, so you can lock it, unlock it, or see its status from anywhere with signal. That's useful if deliveries matter to you, if a dog walker or cleaner comes when you're out, or if you regularly wonder whether you locked up after leaving the house. The reason Wi-Fi uses more power is simple: the lock has to work harder to stay in touch with the network. That doesn't make it bad. It just means the convenience is tied to a heavier battery load and a setup that depends more on your router, signal strength, and app working properly.

Hub-based systems sit between those two. The lock uses a lower-power connection at the door, and a hub inside the house handles the long-distance communication. In real life, that can be a good fit for a larger house, a detached garage entry, or a front door that doesn't get strong Wi-Fi on its own. It can also make sense if you already use a broader smart-home system. If your household wants the fewest moving parts, Bluetooth is often enough. If remote control is the whole point, Wi-Fi makes sense. If you want remote access without asking the lock itself to do all the work, a hub is worth a look.

### Codes are the real advantage over a key

The part people end up using every day isn't the app screen. It's the keypad and the ability to give each person their own code. That matters more because it changes how you control access in real life. A family member can have one code, the cleaner another, a contractor another, and a guest their own short-term code. If somebody loses a code, changes jobs, or no longer needs to come by, you remove that one code instead of changing the whole setup or getting new keys made for everybody.

That only works if you set it up the right way. Don't give multiple people the same code just because it's easy to remember. If the cleaner and the dog walker both use 2580, you have no idea who came in, and if one person should lose access, you end up shutting out both. Separate codes let you keep things clean and simple. They also help you avoid the common problem where an old worker, former tenant, or frequent guest still has a way in long after they should.

The other good habit is not reusing the same code everywhere. We see people use one favorite four-digit number for the front door, alarm, garage, and phone. That's convenient right up until somebody learns it. Treat door codes like house keys: specific to one place and one purpose. If your son needs entry after school, his code should be his code for that door, not the same number your contractor used last season or the same one you punch in at another property. That's the real practical advantage of a smart lock. Not better graphics in an app, but better control over who can enter and when.

### What happens if the company disappears

A smart lock can outlive the company that made the app, and that's not a rare thought experiment. Brands get sold, apps stop getting updates, cloud services get shut down, and phones move on to new operating systems. That does not automatically turn the lock on your door into junk. The important question is simpler: if the app goes away, what still works at the door itself? On a good setup, the basic job of locking and unlocking still works from the keypad, the interior turn piece, and any local programming built into the lock. If those core functions depend on a server somewhere else, you're betting your front door on a business decision you don't control.

This is why we tell people to separate "smart features" from "door functions." Remote alerts, activity history, voice assistant links, and unlocking from another town all usually depend on the manufacturer's app and servers. If that service ends, those extras may disappear even though the hardware still has power. Local functions are different. A lock that stores codes in the lock itself and lets you manage at least the basics without an internet connection is usually the safer buy. It gives you a usable lock even if your Wi-Fi is out, your phone is replaced, or the brand stops supporting older models.

Around Cecil County, we've seen plenty of smart devices become ordinary devices after support fades, and that's not always a problem if the ordinary device still does the main job well. Before you buy, look for plain language in the manual about offline operation, local code storage, and whether initial setup or future changes require an account. If a lock needs the company's servers for everyday ownership, not just for extra features, that's a weaker long-term choice. The fewer outside systems your door depends on, the fewer ways it can let you down.

### Renting, landlords and shared entrances

If you rent, start with permission before you buy anything. A lot of tenants assume a smart lock is like changing a shower head. Sometimes it is, sometimes it isn't. The landlord may have rules about matching hardware, fire code, master key systems, or what can be changed on an exterior door. Get approval in writing, and make sure the lock you choose can be removed without leaving extra holes, a changed strike, or visible marks on the door. Keep the original lock, screws, strike, and any trim in a labeled bag. That matters because moving out usually means putting the door back exactly the way you found it, not "close enough." If the old hardware gets lost, a simple swap turns into a hunt for parts that fit the old prep and finish.

For landlords, smart locks can make turnover easier, but only if you think past the app. The real advantage is controlling access between tenants without wondering how many copies of the old key are still out there. A good setup lets you end old user access cleanly, issue a fresh code for the next tenant, and keep a physical record of what hardware is on each unit. That only works if the lock is installed properly and the door closes and latches the way it should. If the fit is poor, your management gets harder, not easier, because every battery warning or failed lock event becomes a maintenance call.

Shared entrances are a separate problem. If you live in an apartment building, duplex, or converted house near Elkton where one outside door serves more than one occupant, that door usually isn't yours alone to change. It affects every resident, visitors, deliveries, emergency access, and sometimes the building's code compliance. Even in a small multi-unit setup off Pulaski Highway, the communal door needs a building-level plan, not one tenant's gadget choice. Your own unit door may be a good place for a smart lock. The shared entrance usually needs a different kind of access system altogether.

## What Counts as a Locksmith Emergency?

Source: https://deluxelocksmiths.com/blog/what-counts-as-a-locksmith-emergency/

16,000 lockouts a day nationwide. Most aren't emergencies. Here's how to tell which pile you're in.

By the Deluxe Locksmith team September 11, 2026

16,000 lockouts a day nationwide. Most aren't emergencies. Here's how to tell which pile you're in.

16,000 lockouts a day. That's the U.S. average, home and car combined. AAA alone handles around 4 million of those calls a year, according to the Locksmith Industry Statistics report (Locksmith Plus, 2025). Most aren't emergencies. A few are. The trick is telling them apart before you're standing on a porch at 9pm deciding what to do next.

Skimming? Here's the gist. Real emergency means safety risk, or no safe way to just wait it out. Not inconvenience. Break-ins, unsafe lockouts, snapped keys jamming a lock, those count. Sticky deadbolts don't. Deluxe Locksmith runs same-day, Sunday through Friday, across Cecil/Harford County MD and New Castle/Kent County DE. Closed Saturdays, plan around it.

### What Actually Qualifies as a Locksmith Emergency?

Short version: a lock failure that creates a safety risk, or leaves you with no safe way to secure your property right now. A damaged door after a break-in. A lock that won't hold overnight. Being stuck somewhere unsafe. Not a jammed key that's just annoying.

People treat "urgent" and "emergency" as the same word. They're not. Mix them up and you either pay extra for an after-hours rush you didn't need, or you wait on something you shouldn't have. Sticky deadbolt? Fine till Tuesday. Door that won't close after someone kicked it in? Not fine, and if you're staring at that situation right now, here's what not to do when you're locked out before help arrives.

#### Break-Ins and Damaged Entry Points

779,542. That's how many burglaries the FBI recorded nationwide in 2024, and 72% of them hit single-family homes (Home Invasion Statistics, Get Safe and Sound, citing FBI Crime Data Explorer, 2024). About 62% involved forced entry, someone prying, kicking, or drilling their way through a door or lock. Door damaged? Frame splintered? That's same-day, full stop. A house sitting open overnight isn't a "we'll get to it" problem.

Call the police first. Always. Once the scene's cleared, then call a locksmith. And don't try to force a busted lock shut yourself, it almost never holds, and now you've made the actual repair harder.

#### Being Locked Out Somewhere Unsafe

Not every lockout is an emergency. Locked out of your car in a well-lit driveway at 8pm? Annoying, not urgent. Locked out of your house at night with nobody around to let you in, or stuck outside a vehicle somewhere isolated? Different story. The location changes the math.

This is exactly why dispatch routes by location, not by who picks up the phone first. Whoever's closest gets the call. When someone's standing outside in the dark, that difference is minutes, not an afterthought.

#### A Broken Key in the Lock or Ignition

A snapped key is its own kind of emergency. No safety angle needed, just a door that won't lock or a car that won't start. Don't reach for pliers. Digging at a broken key with the wrong tool almost always pushes it deeper or chews up the cylinder, and then you're paying for two problems instead of one. If it's the only copy you had, what to do when you lose your only car key walks through the rest of it.

#### Storefront and Commercial Break-Ins

Commercial break-ins run on their own clock. An open storefront overnight isn't just a repair job, it's an invitation for round two, plus inventory loss and an insurance headache waiting to happen. Damaged door, cracked frame, busted commercial-grade lock, even if nothing was actually stolen: fix it same-day. Not next week, and not because we'd rather bill you sooner, but because storefront doors fail in predictable ways once they've been forced once.

### While You're Waiting

A few things help while you wait. Stay somewhere lit and populated if you're locked out. Just don't stand in a dark parking lot scrolling your phone for twenty minutes. If a break-in happened, leave the damaged door alone, both for the evidence and because touching it rarely helps. Broken key in a lock? Same rule: leave it.

One more thing for homes specifically. If the door won't fully secure, staying put until the technician shows up beats leaving the place open all night.

### The Stuff That Can Actually Wait

Most lock issues aren't emergencies. A sticky deadbolt. A lock that's gotten slow to turn. Swapping in a smart lock, or rekeying after you've moved in but the old locks still work fine, which is really a question of rekey or replace, how to tell which one you need. Real needs, sure, but not urgent ones. Book the next available slot and move on with your day.

Worn-out storefront hardware fits here too, as long as it still latches at closing time. The moment it stops latching, though, that's same-day again.

### How Fast Can You Actually Expect a Response?

Here's the honest answer first: Deluxe Locksmith isn't 24-hour. Sunday through Thursday, 7am to 10pm. Friday, 7am to 3:30pm. Closed Saturdays. Inside those hours, though, dispatch sends the nearest available technician, which is why same-day response actually holds up across Elkton and roughly 38 surrounding towns in Cecil County MD, Harford County MD, New Castle County DE, and Kent County DE.

Outside those hours? Plan for the next window. And if it's a safety issue right now, call law enforcement in the meantime, not us.

### Frequently Asked Questions

#### Is a car lockout always an emergency?

Mostly, no. AAA handles roughly 4 million car lockout calls a year and most of them are just annoying, not urgent (Locksmith Industry Statistics, Locksmith Plus, 2025). The location's what flips it, unsafe surroundings, or nowhere safe to just wait it out.

#### Should I try to force open a lock myself during a break-in?

Don't. You'll likely wreck the cylinder or frame worse than it already is. Secure the scene. Call police. Locksmith comes after, once it's actually safe.

#### Does Deluxe Locksmith offer 24-hour emergency service?

No. Hours are Sunday-Thursday 7am-10pm, Friday 7am-3:30pm. Closed Saturdays, full stop. Same-day still works inside that window because dispatch sends whoever's closest.

#### What should I do if my key breaks inside the ignition?

Skip the household tools, that's the short version. You need actual extraction tools or you'll damage the cylinder further. A mobile locksmith pulls it out on-site, no extra damage.

#### Can a locksmith get into my home without damaging the door?

Usually. Non-destructive methods come first, whenever the lock and door allow it. Covers most homes.

## What to do when you lose your only car key

Source: https://deluxelocksmiths.com/blog/what-to-do-when-you-lose-your-only-car-key/

Losing every copy feels like a disaster. It is a solvable problem, and here is the order to solve it in.

By the Deluxe Locksmith team August 7, 2026

Losing every copy feels like a disaster. It is a solvable problem, and here is the order to solve it in.

### First, stop retracing your steps

The mistake we see all the time is people burning a big part of the day searching everywhere, getting more stressed, and only calling once the car has to be moved, work is starting, or the store parking lot is closing. That makes a bad situation feel worse than it needs to. Do one proper search, not ten half-searches. Check the obvious places twice because keys do turn up in plain sight: yesterday's coat pocket, the jeans you wore last night, the bag you switched out of, the cup holder, the door pocket, and the space under the seat rail where a key can slide and disappear.

Then stop and treat the key as gone. That matters because once you decide it is missing, you start solving the problem instead of losing more time to hopeful guesses. People usually don't "misplace" their only car key in some mysterious way. It tends to be somewhere boring and specific, or it's genuinely lost outside the car. We often hear the same places over and over: a shop's lost property counter, a counter at a gas station on Pulaski Highway, the pocket of a coat left at someone else's house, or down between the seat and console where your hand can't quite reach.

If you've checked the car carefully, checked what you wore, checked where you last paid for something or took keys out of your hand, that's enough. Keep looking later if you want, but don't hold up the fix while you chase a maybe. The reason is simple: searching gets less useful the longer it goes on. You start rechecking the same places and missing the practical next step. A calm, deliberate search helps. An exhausted one usually doesn't. Treating the key as gone early is what gets you back in control.

### What a locksmith needs to know before setting off

Before we roll out, the biggest help you can give us is the exact year, make, and model of the vehicle. "Honda Civic" is not enough by itself. A 2012 Civic and a 2020 Civic may use different key blanks, different chip systems, and different programming steps. The same goes for trim changes inside one model line. That information tells us what keyway we're cutting, whether the car uses a transponder, and which programming tools need to be on the van instead of back at the shop.

We also need to know whether any working key exists anywhere, even if it's not with you. A spare sitting at home, at work, or with a family member changes the job. If there is a working key, some vehicles can be set up differently than if every key is gone. It also matters if the old key is truly lost or just locked in another place, because that affects what we prepare for before heading to your car.

Tell us whether the vehicle can stay where it is for now. A car in your driveway in Elkton is one thing. A car stuck in a tow-away lot off Route 40 is another. If it can't stay, we need to know that up front so we can plan the visit around access, parking, and what equipment has to come with us that day.

Finally, tell us what kind of key the car uses: a plain blade key, a remote-head key with buttons built in, or a push-to-start fob. If you're not sure, say that. We can usually narrow it down from the vehicle information. This matters because those are not interchangeable jobs. The blank is different, the electronics are different, and the programming equipment is different. Good information on the front end keeps us from showing up with the wrong parts for your vehicle.

### How a new key is actually made when there is nothing to copy

If there's no spare key to copy, we don't guess. We have to originate a key, which means rebuilding the key's pattern from the car itself. On some vehicles, that starts by reading the lock wafers in a door or ignition cylinder so we can work out the exact cuts the original key had. On others, we can pull the factory key code from the vehicle information and use that to produce the correct pattern. The reason this matters is simple: the metal blade has to match the lock precisely or it won't turn smoothly, and forcing a close-enough key is how locks get damaged.

Once we have that pattern, we cut a blank key to those exact depths and spaces. That is the mechanical side of the job. If your car uses a basic metal key only, that cut key may be all that's needed to operate the locks and ignition. But most vehicles on the road in Cecil County and around Elkton use a transponder chip, a remote head key, or a push-to-start fob that has to be recognized by the vehicle's anti-theft system.

That's the second job: programming. A newly cut key can open the door and still not start the engine if the immobilizer does not see the right chip data. We connect programming equipment to the vehicle, add the new key or fob to the system, and verify that the car accepts it for starting. If it's a remote or smart key, we also sync the lock, unlock, trunk, or proximity functions if the vehicle uses them. Cutting and programming are separate steps, and both have to happen for a complete working replacement.

### Transponder keys, remote heads and push-to-start

Not every lost car key is the same job. Some older vehicles use a plain blade key, which is purely mechanical. If the cuts on the blade match the locks and ignition, the car will turn. A transponder key looks similar from the outside, but inside the head there is a chip. That chip has to be recognized by the vehicle's anti-theft system or the engine will not start, even if the key turns perfectly. That's why two keys that look almost the same can require completely different tools and steps.

A remote head key takes that transponder setup and adds lock, unlock, trunk, or panic buttons in the head of the key. So now there are two jobs going on at once: the key has to be cut correctly, and the electronics have to be matched so the buttons and the start function work the way they should. Push-to-start vehicles are different again. They use a proximity fob that talks to the car when the fob is nearby. There may still be an emergency insert key hidden inside for the door, but starting the vehicle depends on programming the fob to the car, not just cutting metal.

This is why we ask for the year, make, and model right away, and sometimes for the VIN as well. Carmakers changed systems constantly, even between trim levels and mid-year production changes. A 2008 version of a model may use one system and a 2009 may use another. The equipment needed for a basic metal key is not the same equipment needed to program a chip key or pair a proximity fob. If your car is sitting in a lot off Pulaski Highway or at home in Elkton, getting the vehicle details first is what lets us show up prepared to make the right kind of key, not guess.

### Why the dealership is not your only option

A lot of drivers assume the dealership is the automatic answer, but that is not always how this works in real life. The biggest problem is simple: a dealer will often want the vehicle brought to them before they can do anything. If you have lost the only key, that usually means arranging a tow first. That adds another step because the car cannot be driven there, and on some vehicles it cannot even be shifted easily without the right key present. An automotive locksmith works where the car is parked, whether that is at home, at work, or in a lot off Pulaski Highway.

That matters because making a key is not just about handing you a blank. On many vehicles, the work starts at the car. We verify the vehicle, access the lock or vehicle data needed to create the key, cut it, and then program it if the car uses a chip, remote head, or proximity system. The reason mobile service helps is that the vehicle is right there for testing. If something needs to sync with the immobilizer or the remote functions need to be checked, it can be done on site instead of moving the car around just to begin the process.

That said, it is better to be straight with you than pretend every car is the same. Some very new vehicles, certain luxury models, and some high-security systems really do require dealer-only tools, factory authorization, or software access that an independent locksmith may not have. If your vehicle falls into that category, we will say so plainly. But many cars on the road in Cecil County and nearby Delaware can be handled by a qualified automotive locksmith at the vehicle, which is why the dealership is one option, not the only one.

### If the car is somewhere it cannot stay

If the car is in a spot where it can't sit for long, say that first when you call. Don't just say you're locked out of driving it. Tell us exactly what kind of spot it's in: a pay-and-display bay that's about to expire, a permit-only street, a garage with a closing gate, or a road with tow-away restrictions. That matters because a car stranded in a private lot off Pulaski Highway is a different problem than one sitting where enforcement is active. If there's a posted sign, read it to us word for word if you can. Tell us the address, the lot name, the level or section if it's a garage, and whether the car is blocking anyone or boxed in. That helps us prioritize jobs based on the real risk to the vehicle, not just who sounds most stressed on the phone.

While you're waiting, deal with the parking situation separately instead of assuming the key problem will be solved before enforcement becomes an issue. If it's a metered or app-based space, extend it if the rules allow. If it's a private car park that closes, call the operator or attendant and explain that the vehicle can't be moved because all keys are missing. Ask what they want you to do and whether they can note the plate number. In a permit area or restricted street, contact the local parking office or non-emergency line and ask whether there is any temporary option to avoid a ticket or tow. Don't leave a handwritten note on the dash and assume that will protect you. Sometimes it helps, often it doesn't.

Stay with the car if the location is risky, especially in a garage near the Wilmington station area or anywhere a gate may come down. Keep your phone on, watch for callbacks, and be ready to answer questions about the exact location. The key issue and the parking issue are two separate problems. Treating them that way gives you the best chance of keeping a bad day from getting worse.

### What to do about the old key

If the missing key could be tied back to your car, treat it as a security problem, not just a lockout. A plain key lost somewhere random is one thing. A key lost with your registration, a gym tag with your plate number on it, a work badge, or anything that points to your address or the vehicle is different. Now the issue is not only getting back into the car. It is stopping that old key from being useful to the wrong person.

Re-coding the locks is what fixes that. On a traditional mechanical key, that means changing the lock so the old cuts no longer match. On many vehicles, it can also mean removing the missing key from the car's security memory so it will not start the vehicle even if someone still has the metal key or fob. The reason to do it is simple: if the key is in somebody else's hand and they can identify the car, the problem does not end when a new key is made. It ends when the missing key no longer works.

You usually should re-code if the key was stolen, if it disappeared from a place where people could connect it to your vehicle, or if your wallet, registration, insurance card, house keys, or address were lost with it. We also strongly recommend it if the vehicle sits in an open lot, apartment parking area, or anywhere a stranger could walk up and try the key.

You may not need re-coding if the key was destroyed, dropped into water and recovered, or clearly lost in a way that cannot be linked back to you or the car. For example, a key lost on its own somewhere along Pulaski Highway is not the same risk as a key lost with identifying documents in a parking lot near your home in Elkton. If you are not sure, tell us exactly what was lost with the key and where it happened. That tells us whether this is just a replacement job or a security cleanup too.

### Get a spare made the same week

The real reason a lost car key turns into a full-blown problem is simple: there wasn't a backup. Once you're back in the car with a working key again, don't treat that as the finish line. Get a spare made that same week, while everything is still fresh and the vehicle is available. One working key means the next loss, lockout, or damaged key puts you right back in the same spot. Two keys changes the whole situation. If one disappears, breaks, or gets locked in the car, you still have a way to drive, move the vehicle, and avoid turning one bad day into another.

There's also a big difference between copying a key that works and creating one when nothing is left. With a working key in hand, we're duplicating a known, proven key. The cuts can be matched directly, and on vehicles that use a chip or remote functions, the existing key gives us a solid starting point. When there is no key at all, the job becomes more involved because the key has to be originated from the vehicle instead of copied from a sample that already works. That's why the smart move is to make the duplicate while the first key is still in service, not after it's gone.

Where you keep that spare matters. Don't put it on the same ring as the everyday key, because losing one ring means losing both. Keep it somewhere separate and consistent: at home in a drawer you'll remember, in a small lockbox, or with someone you trust nearby. If you commute through places like Elkton or up Route 40, think about where you would actually need access from if your main key vanished. The best spare is the one you can get to without a second emergency.

## Why storefront doors fail

Source: https://deluxelocksmiths.com/blog/why-storefront-doors-fail/

An aluminium storefront door opens hundreds of times a day. Here is what wears out first, and why.

By the Deluxe Locksmith team August 11, 2026

An aluminium storefront door opens hundreds of times a day. Here is what wears out first, and why.

### Volume is the whole story

A front door at a house might see a handful of trips in the morning, a few at night, and not much in between. A storefront door is a different machine entirely. Staff comes in, customers come in and out all day, deliveries hit the door, and people lean on it, push it, pull it, and let it swing wider and harder than it was ever meant to at a home. That cycle count is what changes everything. Hardware doesn't wear out because it exists. It wears out because it repeats the same movement over and over under load, and a business door repeats that movement far more than a residential lockset, hinge, or closer ever will.

That's why commercial-grade parts exist. They're built for a higher number of cycles, heavier door leaves, stronger springs, thicker pivots, better bearings, and hardware that can take abuse without going sloppy right away. On a busy aluminum storefront, the stress is constant. Every opening puts force through the same points: the pivot, the closer arm, the latch, the fasteners, the frame prep. If one part is undersized, the rest of the door pays for it. What looks fine on a side door at home often starts showing play, drag, looseness, or incomplete latching fast when it's asked to do storefront duty.

We see this a lot in small retail spaces and office entries around places like Elkton and along Pulaski Highway: someone tries to solve a commercial problem with residential hardware because the parts seem similar at a glance. They usually aren't. The mounting, backset, door thickness, cycle rating, and load handling are different for a reason. A lighter-duty part may bolt on, but it won't live long in a door that opens hundreds of times a day. The result is repeat failure, and usually more wear on the surrounding hardware too.

### The parts that go first

On a busy aluminum storefront door, the weight is riding on the pivots and the top and bottom arms every time that door swings. Those parts are the door's support system. The bottom pivot carries the load, the top pivot keeps the slab tracking where it should, and the arms tie the door to the frame so it can move in a controlled path instead of twisting. When they start wearing out, the door usually tells you before it quits. You may see the gap at the top change from one side to the other, the bottom edge start kissing the threshold, or the latch stop lining up cleanly. A door that suddenly feels heavier, drags, or has a little sag in it is often showing wear in those support points, not a problem with the lock itself.

The lock parts take a different kind of abuse. Hook bolts and mortise cylinders are worked over and over, all day, by staff, deliveries, and closing routines. The hook bolt is the part that throws into the frame and actually secures many storefront doors; the mortise cylinder is the keyed cylinder that turns the lock body inside the stile. They wear because small internal parts are doing the same job constantly, and because a slightly out-of-line door makes the lock work harder every turn. Early signs are usually subtle: the key starts needing a wiggle, the thumbturn feels stiff, the bolt does not throw all the way without pulling the door, or the key comes out rough instead of smooth.

Thresholds wear because they take every footstep, cart wheel, bit of grit, and the bottom edge of the door when alignment starts drifting. On many storefronts around Elkton, you can spot a worn threshold by a polished groove, loose fasteners, or sharp edges where the metal has been chewed up. Once that surface is worn down or loosened, the door can scrape, catch, or bounce on closing. That is not just cosmetic wear. It changes how the door meets the frame and adds strain to the hardware above and inside it.

### Alignment is usually the real fault

A storefront door can refuse to lock even when the lock itself is working exactly the way it should. What usually changed is the door position. Aluminum doors get pulled, pushed, leaned on, and slammed all day. Over time the door can sag at the hinges, the frame can shift, or the opening can rack slightly. When that happens, the hook bolt or latch no longer lines up with the keeper in the frame. People assume the key cylinder failed because the key got hard to turn, but the cylinder only turns the mechanism. If the bolt has nowhere clean to land, changing the cylinder solves nothing.

You can often spot the difference before paying for the wrong repair. If the key turns with the door open but not with the door closed, that points to alignment, not a bad cylinder. If you have to lift the pull handle, shove the door, or pull it toward you to get it to lock, that is another strong sign. Look at the gap around the door. A wider gap at the top corner or scrape marks at the threshold usually mean the door has dropped. On Adams Rite style storefront hardware, the hook should enter the keeper smoothly. If it strikes the edge of the keeper, hits low, or barely catches, the problem is geometry.

A worn cylinder usually acts up the same way whether the door is open or closed. The key may bind, stick, or fail to turn the cam at all. An alignment problem changes with pressure on the door. We see this a lot on busy storefronts from Elkton to U.S. 40, especially after the door has been forced a little or the hinges have loosened over time. The right repair is to correct the sag or misalignment first, then test the lock. Otherwise you end up replacing a part that was never the reason the door stopped securing.

### What a door closer is actually doing

A door closer is the hydraulic arm at the top of the door that controls how the door returns after someone opens it. It is not just there to make the door shut. It manages the door through different parts of the swing so it closes in a controlled way, pulls itself tight at the end, and does not fly open hard enough to damage the frame, glass, or wall. On a busy aluminum storefront, that control matters because the door is being pushed and pulled all day by customers, staff, carts, wind, and people carrying things who are not guiding it gently.

Closing speed is the main sweep of the door as it comes back toward the frame. If that setting is too fast, the door slams and you hear it across the store. That shock gets transferred into the closer, hinges, frame, and lock every single cycle. If closing speed is too slow, the door drifts back lazily and may never get enough momentum to finish the job. Latching speed is the last few inches of travel, where the latch has to enter the strike and seat properly. If latching speed is too weak, the door stops short, bounces, or sits there looking closed when it is not actually secured. That is not a nuisance at closing time. It means the storefront may be left unlocked, and someone can pull it open from outside without forcing anything.

Backcheck is the braking action when the door is opened hard. It slows the door before it reaches the end of its swing. When backcheck is set wrong, or not working at all, a gust or a strong push can send the door straight into the wall, the glass, or the stop. That is why a closer has more than one adjustment. Each function is doing a different job, and when one is off, the door tells on itself.

### Panic hardware is a life-safety item

An exit device is not just another piece of door hardware. It's the bar people push when they need to get out, and that makes it a life-safety item first and a repair item second. These devices are part of what gets looked at during inspections, and they are not optional on doors that are meant to have them. If the bar doesn't move cleanly, if the latch doesn't release every time, or if the device has been tied back or propped so it stays unlatched, that door is no longer doing the job it was installed to do.

Sticking or binding usually means the device is being forced to work against another problem, but the symptom still matters on its own. If people have to shove hard, hit the bar twice, or lean into the door to get out, that is a warning sign. In a normal rush of traffic, staff may work around it without thinking much about it. In an emergency, nobody has the extra attention for a door that only works if you know its trick. Panic hardware has to release plainly and predictably, every time, for every person using it.

A propped device is its own problem too. Sometimes a business keeps the latch retracted because the door is hard to open, deliveries are constant, or the bar has started dragging. That may keep traffic moving for the moment, but it also leaves the opening unsecured and masks wear that keeps getting worse. We see this on busy storefronts from Elkton through the Route 40 corridor: the hardware gets treated like a nuisance instead of a safety system. That's why it shouldn't wait for the next unrelated service call. If the exit device is sticking, binding, loose, damaged, or held open, it needs attention because it affects safe egress every time that door is used.

### Weather, grit and the seasons

A storefront door doesn't live in one condition all year. In summer, the aluminum frame and door slab heat up and grow slightly. In winter, they contract. Those small changes matter because storefront hardware is built around tight clearances. A door that had just enough room at the head, jamb, or threshold in August can start rubbing once cold weather shrinks one part more than another. The frame, the glass, the rails, the threshold, even the fasteners all react a little differently to temperature. That's why a door can seem fine for months, then suddenly feel heavy, drag, or stop latching cleanly after the first real cold stretch.

The bottom of the opening takes the worst of the weather. Dirt, sand, and parking-lot grit get walked straight into the threshold and lower pivot area. That debris doesn't just sit there. It packs into corners, grinds at moving parts, and changes how the door rides over the threshold. Add road salt, damp air, and tracked-in slush, and the lower hardware stays wet longer than the rest of the opening. Around places near Route 40, we see a lot of doors where the trouble starts low: corrosion on fasteners, buildup in the saddle, and drag that gets worse every time the door cycles.

Winter sticking usually isn't because the door suddenly "went bad." More often, summer heat was masking a marginal condition. The door had just enough clearance, the threshold already had some grit in it, and the lower parts were already starting to wear. Then cold weather tightens the margins. Seals get stiffer, metal moves, moisture hangs around the bottom, and the same door that worked through July starts catching in January. That seasonal change is a clue. It tells us to look at how the whole opening is reacting to weather, not just the spot where you feel it rubbing.

### What to check before you call

Before you call, do one simple test with the door open a crack: pull it fully into the frame by hand, then try the key. If the key turns freely only when you're holding the door snug, the lock usually isn't the real problem. That points to the door not landing where the lock expects it to land. The cylinder and key may be fine, but the latch or hook is being forced against the keeper instead of lining up cleanly with it. If the key is still stiff even with the door held tight, that tells us to look harder at the lock body, cylinder, keyway, or internal wear instead of blaming alignment first.

Next, stand back and look at the gaps around the door. Daylight at the top on one side, or a bigger gap at the bottom than the top, usually means the door is sitting out of square in the opening. On aluminum storefront doors, small changes in that gap matter. The lock has very little tolerance, so a door that has dropped, twisted, or shifted can make good hardware act bad. Then check whether the hook actually meets the keeper where it should. If the hook hits the face of the keeper, slides under it, or barely catches, that's a strong sign the door and frame are no longer meeting in the right place.

Last, watch the closer do its job without anyone pushing or pulling the door. It should bring the door all the way shut on its own and leave it fully seated in the frame. If it stops short, bounces, or needs a shove at the end, the door may never reach the position the lock needs. That's why a lock can seem unreliable at the front of a busy shop off Pulaski Highway even when the key and cylinder are not worn out. These checks won't fix the problem, but they do tell you whether you're dealing with lock trouble, alignment trouble, or both.

### Where we do this

We cover Northeast Maryland & Delaware. If you want the detail for your own town rather than the general advice above, start here:

- Locksmith in North East, MD
- Locksmith in Conowingo, MD
- Locksmith in Forest Hill, MD
- Locksmith in Bear, DE
- Locksmith in Townsend, DE
- Locksmith in Clayton, DE

## You just bought a house. Rekey it before you unpack

Source: https://deluxelocksmiths.com/blog/you-just-bought-a-house-rekey-it/

You have no idea how many copies of that key exist. Neither does the seller.

By the Deluxe Locksmith team August 9, 2026

You have no idea how many copies of that key exist. Neither does the seller.

### The keys you were handed are not the only keys

At closing, you usually get a small set of keys and a garage remote or two. That only tells you what made it to the table that day. It does not tell you how many copies were made over the years, who kept one, or which old key still works. Most houses collect extra keys the same way they collect old paint cans and spare parts: one at a time, for perfectly normal reasons, and then nobody keeps track.

The obvious people are the previous owners and anyone in their family who had regular access. Adult kids may have had a key. Parents may have had one for emergencies. Neighbors sometimes get a spare to feed pets or water plants. Then there are the work keys. Contractors, handymen, cleaners, landscapers, dog walkers, house sitters, babysitters, and home health aides are all people who might have been trusted with access at some point. Real estate agents may have had keys during showings. If the home was ever rented, previous tenants may still have copies, and so might a property manager or maintenance person from years back.

That does not mean the seller is hiding something from you. Most of the time they are not. They genuinely do not know where every copy ended up, especially if they have owned the place for a long time or inherited it from someone else. Keys get loaned out, copied at a hardware store, left in junk drawers, attached to old keychains, or never returned after a job. We see this all the time in houses around Elkton: the keys handed over are the known keys, not all keys.

That is the real reason to deal with the locks right away. You are not accusing anyone of bad intent. You are closing off unknown access from people who may still have a working key and may not even remember they do.

### Rekeying is not the same as replacing

A rekey keeps the lock you already have and changes what key operates it. Inside the cylinder are small pins cut to match the grooves of a specific key. We take that cylinder apart and reset those pins to a different pattern, then cut new keys to match. After that, the old keys may still slide in, but they won't turn the lock. The outside hardware stays the same: same lock body, same handle, same finish, same look on the door.

That matters because replacing hardware is a different job. New locks can mean pulling trim, swapping handles or deadbolts, lining up screw holes, and sometimes dealing with doors that have settled and never fit quite right to begin with. If you like the hardware that's there, rekeying lets you keep it. There's no need to change the style or try to match finishes across every exterior door just to make old keys stop working.

Rekeying is usually the cleaner option because it changes the part that controls access without changing the whole assembly. On a house in Elkton or out toward Route 40, that often means less disturbance right when you've already got movers, boxes, and utility appointments stacked up. We're working on the cylinder, not redesigning the door. If the existing lock is solid and functioning the way it should, rekeying solves the actual problem: unknown keys out in the world.

It's also worth knowing what rekeying does not do. It doesn't fix a worn-out lock, a loose deadbolt, or hardware that sticks, wobbles, or fails to latch properly. If the lock itself is in good shape, rekeying is the direct answer. If the hardware is damaged or unreliable, that's when replacement starts to make more sense.

### The doors people forget

Most people think about the front door and stop there. That's the one they use every day, so it feels like the obvious priority. But the locks that get missed are usually the ones someone could use without being seen right away: the side door into the garage, the basement door, the shed, the gate, even the mailbox. On an older property, those locks often got added at different times by different owners, and they may still be on older keys the seller hasn't had in years.

That matters because one forgotten lock can undo the whole point of rekeying. If every main entry is updated but the back basement door still works on an old key, you haven't really closed the loop. The same goes for a garage service door or a gate that gives someone access to the back of the house. We've seen homes around Elkton where the front was handled properly, but a side entry or detached shed was still wide open to anyone holding an old copy.

Before you book the work, walk the property and write every lock down. Start at the front, then go around the house and outbuildings in a full loop. Check both sides of the garage, any walkout basement entry, fence gates, storage doors, and the mailbox if it locks. If there's a door you only use once in a while, that's exactly the one people forget. A quick list helps us make sure nothing gets skipped, and it helps you avoid finding the one old-key door after you've already moved everything in.

### Getting every door onto one key

If the locks on your house use compatible cylinders, we can usually rekey them so one key works the front door, back door, side door, and the door from the garage into the house. That's called keyed alike. The big advantage is simple: less confusion. You're not standing in the driveway with a ring full of similar keys trying each one, and everyone in the house knows which key is the house key. It also makes life easier when you're giving a copy to a spouse, a dog walker, or a family member helping during the move.

The part people don't think about is what happens if that one key goes missing. If a single key opens every exterior door, then losing it means the whole property is exposed, not just one entry. That matters more for some households than others. If you've got teens carrying keys, a lot of people coming and going, or a key that's likely to be left in a gym locker, on a jobsite, or dropped somewhere along Pulaski Highway, one-key convenience may not be the smartest setup.

In those cases, two keys often make more sense. A common setup is one key for the main entry doors you use every day, and a different key for a less-used door like the side or basement entry. Another is keeping the house on one key and a detached garage or workshop on another. You still cut down the clutter, but you limit what one lost key can do. When we rekey a new house, we usually talk through how you actually use the doors, not just how many locks are on them. That's how you end up with a setup that's convenient without being careless.

### When replacement really is the right answer

Rekeying only makes sense if the lock itself is still worth keeping. The pins can be changed, but that does nothing for a deadbolt that's loose, badly worn, or built too light for an outside door. If the key has to be jiggled, the cylinder binds, the latch doesn't move cleanly, or the bolt only works if you pull or shove the door, that's not really a key-control problem anymore. That's a worn lock, a door alignment issue, or both. Rekeying a lock in that condition can leave you with a fresh key and the same daily headache.

We also tell people to replace locks that show real weather damage. On houses near the water in Kent County, and even plenty of places around Elkton, we see exterior hardware with corrosion inside the cylinder, rust on the screws, pitting on the face, and springs that no longer return the key smoothly. Once the internal parts are worn or corroded, rekeying won't restore strength or reliability. The lock may still turn today, but it's more likely to stick, fail, or stop working at the worst time.

Replacement is also the right move when the lock is the wrong grade or wrong type for the way the house is used now. A basic knob lock used as the main security on an exterior door, a deadbolt with excessive play, a mismatched setup that leaves one door easier to force than the rest, or hardware that no longer fits the household all point toward replacement. If you want a proper deadbolt where there isn't one, if the existing lock has obvious slop, if screws no longer bite tightly, or if the trim is cracking around the mounting points, the lock is past the point where rekeying is the smart answer. In those cases, replacing it fixes the actual problem instead of just changing which key operates it.

### The strike plate is where most doors actually fail

A lot of people picture a burglar "beating the lock," but that's usually not what gives way. On most house doors, the deadbolt is still sitting there in one piece after a kick. What breaks is the wood around it. The short screws that hold the strike plate often bite into the jamb or trim, not the solid framing behind it. So the bolt stays strong, but the frame splits and the door opens anyway.

That's why one of the smartest upgrades after a move has nothing to do with a fancier lock. It's making sure the strike plate is fastened with long screws that reach through the jamb and into the framing stud behind it. That changes what the force is hitting. Instead of asking a thin strip of wood to hold the door shut, you're tying that hardware into the structure of the wall. On a front door or side entry, that difference matters a lot more than most people realize.

We see plenty of homes around Elkton where the lock itself is decent, but the strike side was never reinforced. Builders and handymen often use whatever screws came in the box, and those are frequently too short to do the real job. If the door is already a little loose, out of square, or rubbing, that can make the weak point even weaker. A proper strike plate setup helps the deadbolt do what you think it's already doing.

It's not glamorous. You won't show it off after you move in. But if you want the highest-value security upgrade in the house, this is near the top of the list. A strong lock on a weak frame is only half a lock.

### Windows, sliders and the back of the house

Most break-ins don't start at the front door. They start where nobody on the street can see what's happening. Ground-floor windows, patio sliders, and basement doors sit on the quiet side of the house, and that privacy works for an intruder as much as it works for you. New owners usually focus on the keys they were handed and the main entry doors. Meanwhile, a weak window latch in the den, an old slider off the kitchen, or a basement walkout hidden by a fence can be the easier way in.

Patio sliders deserve extra attention because a lot of them are only doing one real job: keeping the door shut, not keeping someone out. If the lock is loose, misaligned, or worn, the door can sometimes be lifted, flexed, or worked open without much noise. A proper slider check means looking at the latch, the track, the rollers, and whether there's secondary protection to stop the panel from being forced or lifted. We also see plenty of houses where the slider hasn't been adjusted in years, so the lock never fully seats even though it looks closed.

Ground-floor and basement windows matter for the same reason: they're often out of sight and rarely tested by the new owner. People assume the lock works because the window closes. That's not the same thing. We find missing sash locks, bent latches, painted-shut hardware, and basement windows that don't secure tightly anymore. The back of the house matters more than the front because it gives cover. If someone can stand behind the house without being noticed, they have time to test a weak slider, push on a window, or work at a basement entry nobody checks until there's a problem. That's why we tell new owners to treat the back side of the property like the primary security line, not the afterthought.

### What to do the same week you move in

Start with the locks that let someone straight into the house. First, have every exterior lock rekeyed so the keys from the closing table are the only ones that work. That means front door, back door, side door, basement door, and any lock on a storm or security door that takes a separate key. Do it first because every other move-in job can wait a little; control of the keys shouldn't. Once that's done, label nothing with your address. If a key gets lost at the grocery store in Elkton, you don't want it coming with directions.

Second, open each exterior door and look at the strike area on the frame. Tight screws, solid wood, and a latch or deadbolt that lines up cleanly matter more than most people think. Third, test every exterior door the way a burglar would. Close it fully, lock it, then push on it with your shoulder. You're checking that the latch actually catches and the door can't be popped open because it was only half-latched or badly aligned. A lot of doors seem locked until pressure shows they aren't really secured.

Fourth, deal with the doors people leave for later: the garage service door, the door from garage to house, shed locks, and any side gate lock if it uses a key. Those are common weak spots because movers are in and out, remotes get handed around, and older keys tend to stay in circulation. Last, decide now who gets a copy and who doesn't. Keep that list short. One spare in a controlled place is better than handing keys to relatives, contractors, neighbors, and dog walkers as the week gets hectic. The fewer copies out there from day one, the fewer problems you inherit later on Route 40 or anywhere else in the county.
